chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2
paragraphs: A lawn before the DUKE'S palace
Enter ROSALIND and CELIA
CELIA. Please, Rosalind, sweet cousin, be cheerful.

ROSALIND. Dear Celia, I'm showing more cheer than I actually feel, and you'd have me even merrier than that? Unless you can teach me to forget a banished father, you can't teach me how to remember any extraordinary pleasure.

CELIA. I can see you don't love me with the full weight that I love you. If my uncle, your banished father, had banished your uncle—the Duke, my father—and you had stayed here with me, I could have taught my love to take your father as my own. You'd have done the same, if the truth of your love for me were as righteously balanced as mine is for you.
ROSALIND. All right, I'll forget my own circumstances and rejoice in yours.

CELIA. You know my father has no child but me, and isn't likely to have any other. Truly, when he dies you'll be his heir. What he took from your father by force, I'll restore to you in affection. On my honor, I will—and if I break that oath, may I turn into a monster. So, my sweet Rose, my dear Rose, be merry.
ROSALIND. From now on I will, cousin, and we'll invent some pastimes. Let's see—what do you think of falling in love?
CELIA. By all means, do—as a sport. But don't love any man in earnest, and don't go further even in sport than you can safely retreat from with an honorable blush.
ROSALIND. What shall our sport be, then?
CELIA. Let's sit and mock the good housewife Fortune off her wheel, so that from now on her gifts will be handed out equally.
ROSALIND. I wish we could. Her favors are terribly misplaced; that generous blind woman makes her worst mistakes in what she gives to women.
CELIA. True—the ones she makes beautiful, she rarely makes virtuous; and the ones she makes virtuous, she makes very ugly.
ROSALIND. No, now you're shifting from Fortune's office to Nature's. Fortune rules over worldly gifts, not over the features Nature gives.
Enter TOUCHSTONE
CELIA. No? When Nature has made a beautiful creature, can't Fortune throw her into the fire? Though Nature has given us wit to mock Fortune, hasn't Fortune sent in this fool to cut off the argument?
ROSALIND. Indeed, Fortune is too tough for Nature here—when Fortune uses one of Nature's naturals to cut off Nature's wit.

CELIA. Perhaps this isn't Fortune's doing either, but Nature's—who, seeing that our natural wits are too dull to reason about such goddesses, has sent this natural to be our whetstone. The dullness of the fool is always the whetstone of wits. Well now, wit! Where are you wandering?
TOUCHSTONE. Mistress, you're to come at once to your father.
CELIA. Were you made the messenger?
TOUCHSTONE. No, on my honor; but I was told to come fetch you.
ROSALIND. Where did you learn that oath, fool?

TOUCHSTONE. From a certain knight who swore by his honor that the pancakes were good, and swore by his honor that the mustard was bad. Now I'll insist the pancakes were bad and the mustard was good—and yet the knight wasn't forsworn.
CELIA. How do you prove that, out of the great heap of your knowledge?
ROSALIND. Yes, indeed, now unmuzzle your wisdom.
TOUCHSTONE. Both of you, step forward—stroke your chins and swear by your beards that I am a rogue.
CELIA. By our beards, if we had any, you are.

TOUCHSTONE. By my roguery, if I had any, then I would be. But if you swear by something that isn't there, you aren't forsworn. Neither was this knight, swearing by his honor—because he never had any. Or if he had any, he had sworn it away long before he ever saw those pancakes or that mustard.
CELIA. Please, who is it that you mean?
TOUCHSTONE. One whom old Frederick, your father, loves.
CELIA. My father's love is enough to honor him. Enough—say no more about him. You'll be whipped for slander one of these days.
TOUCHSTONE. All the more pity that fools may not speak wisely about what wise men do foolishly.
CELIA. By my faith, you're right. Ever since the little wit that fools have was silenced, the little foolishness that wise men have makes a great show. Here comes Monsieur Le Beau.
Enter LE BEAU
ROSALIND. With his mouth full of news.
CELIA. Which he'll stuff into us the way pigeons feed their young.
ROSALIND. Then we'll be crammed with news.
CELIA. All the better—we'll be more marketable. Bon jour, Monsieur Le Beau. What's the news?
LE BEAU. Fair Princess, you've missed some excellent sport.
CELIA. Sport! Of what color?
LE BEAU. What color, madam? How shall I answer that?
ROSALIND. However wit and fortune decide.
TOUCHSTONE. Or however the Destinies decree.
CELIA. Well said—that was laid on with a trowel.
TOUCHSTONE. No, if I don't keep up my rank—
ROSALIND. You lose your old smell.
LE BEAU. You amaze me, ladies. I meant to tell you of some good wrestling that you've missed.
ROSALIND. Still—tell us how the wrestling went.
LE BEAU. I'll tell you the beginning, and if your ladyships
please, you may see the end—for the best is still to come, and they're coming right here, where you are, to perform it.
CELIA. Well then, the beginning—which is dead and buried.
LE BEAU. There comes an old man and his three sons—
CELIA. I could match this beginning with an old tale.
LE BEAU. Three handsome young men, of excellent stature and bearing.
ROSALIND. With notices around their necks: 'Be it known unto all men by these presents'—

LE BEAU. The eldest of the three wrestled with Charles, the Duke's wrestler. In an instant Charles threw him and broke three of his ribs, so there's little hope of life in him. He did the same to the second, and the same to the third. There they lie. The poor old father is making such pitiful lament over them that all the bystanders are weeping in sympathy.
ROSALIND. Alas!
TOUCHSTONE. But what's the sport, monsieur, that the ladies have missed?
LE BEAU. Why, this that I'm telling you about.
TOUCHSTONE. So men can grow wiser every day. It's the first time I ever heard breaking of ribs called sport for ladies.
CELIA. Same for me, I swear.
ROSALIND. But is there anyone else who longs to hear this broken music in his ribs? Is there another fan of rib-breaking out there? Shall we watch this wrestling, cousin?
LE BEAU. You'll have to, if you stay here. This is the spot appointed for the match, and they're ready to begin.
CELIA. Look, here they come. Let's stay and watch.
Flourish. Enter DUKE FREDERICK, LORDS, ORLANDO, CHARLES, and ATTENDANTS
FREDERICK. Get on with it. Since the youth won't be talked out of it, let the danger be on his own stubborn head.
ROSALIND. Is that the man over there?
LE BEAU. The very one, madam.
CELIA. Alas, he's too young—yet he has a successful look.
FREDERICK. Well now, daughter and niece! Have you crept in here to watch the wrestling?
ROSALIND. Yes, my lord—with your permission.
FREDERICK. You won't take much delight in it, I can tell you.
The match is so uneven. Out of pity for the challenger's youth I'd gladly dissuade him, but he won't listen. Speak to him, ladies—see if you can move him.
CELIA. Call him over, good Monsieur Le Beau.
FREDERICK. Do so; I'll step aside.
[DUKE FREDERICK goes apart]
LE BEAU. Monsieur the Challenger, the Princess calls for you.
ORLANDO. I attend on them with all respect and duty.
ROSALIND. Young man, have you challenged Charles the wrestler?
ORLANDO. No, fair Princess—he's the one issuing the general challenge. I come in, like the others, to test the strength of my youth against him.

CELIA. Young gentleman, your spirits are too bold for your years. You've seen brutal proof of this man's strength. If you could see yourself with your own eyes, or know yourself by your own judgment, the fear of the attempt would advise you to a more even match. We beg you, for your own sake, embrace your safety and give up this attempt.
ROSALIND. Please, young sir—your reputation won't suffer for it. We'll make it our request to the Duke that the wrestling not go forward.

ORLANDO. I beg you, don't punish me with your harsh thoughts—I confess I'm very guilty in denying anything to such fair and excellent ladies. But let your fair eyes and gentle wishes go with me into the trial. If I'm defeated, only one is shamed who was never favored. If I'm killed, only one is dead who is willing to die. I'll do my friends no wrong, since I have none to mourn me. I'll do the world no harm, since I have nothing in it. I only fill up a place in the world—a place that may be better filled when I have emptied it.
ROSALIND. The little strength I have, I wish were with you.
CELIA. And mine to add to hers.
ROSALIND. Fare you well. I pray heaven I'm wrong about you!
CELIA. May your heart's desires go with you!
CHARLES. Come on—where's this young gallant who's so eager to lie down on his mother earth?
ORLANDO. Ready, sir—but his will works on a more modest plan than that.
FREDERICK. You'll try only one fall.
CHARLES. No, I assure your Grace, you won't have to talk him into a second—not after the trouble you had urging him out of the first.
ORLANDO. You plan to mock me afterward; you shouldn't have mocked me beforehand. Come on then.
ROSALIND. Now, may Hercules be your strength, young man!
CELIA. I wish I were invisible, to catch that strong fellow by the leg.                                          [They wrestle]
ROSALIND. Oh, excellent young man!
CELIA. If I had a thunderbolt in my eye, I could tell you who'd go down.
[CHARLES is thrown. Shout]
FREDERICK. No more, no more.
ORLANDO. Yes, I beg your Grace—I'm not even out of breath yet.
FREDERICK. How are you, Charles?
LE BEAU. He can't speak, my lord.
FREDERICK. Carry him away. What is your name, young man?
ORLANDO. Orlando, my lord—the youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys.

FREDERICK. I wish you had been the son of some other man. The world thought your father honorable, But I always found him to be my enemy. You would have pleased me better with this deed Had you come from a different house. But fare you well; you're a gallant youth. I wish you had named me a different father. Exeunt DUKE, train, and LE BEAU
CELIA. If I were my father, cousin, would I do this?
ORLANDO. I'm prouder to be Sir Rowland's son, His youngest son—and would not exchange that title To be adopted heir to Frederick.

ROSALIND. My father loved Sir Rowland as his own soul, And all the world shared my father's opinion. Had I known beforehand this young man was his son, I would have added tears to my pleading Before he should have risked himself like this.

CELIA. Gentle cousin, Let us go thank him, and encourage him; My father's rough and envious temper Cuts me to the heart. Sir, you've well deserved; If you keep your promises in love As justly as you've exceeded all promise here, Your mistress will be happy.
ROSALIND. Gentleman,        [Giving him a chain from her neck] Wear this for me—from one who's out of favor with fortune, Who would give more, but her hand lacks the means. Shall we go, cousin?
CELIA. Yes. Fare you well, fair gentleman.
ORLANDO. Can't I even say 'I thank you'? My better parts Are all thrown down; and what stands up here Is only a quintain, a mere lifeless block.
ROSALIND. He calls us back. My pride fell with my fortunes; I'll ask him what he wants. Did you call, sir? Sir, you've wrestled well, and overthrown More than your enemies.
CELIA. Are you coming, cousin?
ROSALIND. I'm with you. Fare you well. Exeunt ROSALIND and CELIA

ORLANDO. What passion hangs these weights on my tongue? I cannot speak to her, though she invited conversation. O poor Orlando, you are overthrown! Either Charles or something weaker has mastered you.
Re-enter LE BEAU

LE BEAU. Good sir, I counsel you in friendship To leave this place. Although you have deserved High commendation, true applause, and love, Yet such is now the Duke's mood That he misconstrues all that you have done. The Duke is moody; what he is, indeed, Is more for you to imagine than for me to say.
ORLANDO. I thank you, sir; and please tell me this: Which of the two was daughter of the Duke Who was here at the wrestling?

LE BEAU. Neither, if we judge by manners; But the smaller one is indeed his daughter; The other is daughter to the banished Duke, And kept here by her usurping uncle To be his daughter's companion; their loves Are dearer than the natural bond of sisters. But I can tell you that lately this Duke Has taken displeasure against his gentle niece, Grounded on no other reason Than that the people praise her for her virtues And pity her for her good father's sake; And on my life, his malice against the lady Will suddenly burst out. Sir, fare you well. Hereafter, in a better world than this, I shall desire more love and knowledge of you.

ORLANDO. I'm much obliged to you; fare you well. Exit LE BEAU So I must pass from the smoke into the fire; From a tyrant Duke to a tyrant brother. But heavenly Rosalind!                                  Exit

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3
paragraphs: The DUKE's palace
Enter CELIA and ROSALIND
CELIA. Why, cousin! Why, Rosalind! Cupid have mercy! Not a word?
ROSALIND. Not one to throw at a dog.
CELIA. No, your words are too precious to waste on mongrels. Throw some of them at me. Come on, lame me with reasons.
ROSALIND. Then there'd be two cousins laid up—one lamed with reasons and the other mad without any.
CELIA. But is this all because of your father?
ROSALIND. No, some of it is because of my child's father. Oh, how full of briars is this working-day world!
CELIA. They're only burs, cousin, thrown on you in holiday foolery. If we don't walk in the well-worn paths, our very petticoats will catch them.
ROSALIND. I could shake those off my coat. But these burs are in my heart.
CELIA. Just cough them away.
ROSALIND. I would try, if a cough of 'hem' could bring him to me.
CELIA. Come on, wrestle with your feelings.
ROSALIND. Oh, they're on the side of a better wrestler than I am.

CELIA. Well, good luck to you! You'll keep trying in time, despite the fall. But putting these jokes aside, let's talk seriously. Is it possible that all of a sudden you've fallen so hard for old Sir Rowland's youngest son?
ROSALIND. The Duke my father loved his father dearly.
CELIA. Does it follow then that you should love his son dearly? By that kind of logic I should hate him, because my father hated his father dearly. Yet I don't hate Orlando.
ROSALIND. No, by my faith—don't hate him, for my sake.
CELIA. Why shouldn't I? Doesn't he deserve to be hated?
Enter DUKE FREDERICK, with LORDS
ROSALIND. Let me love him for that, and you love him because I do. Look, here comes the Duke.
CELIA. With his eyes full of anger.
FREDERICK. Mistress, get out as fast as safety allows, And remove yourself from our court.
ROSALIND. Me, uncle?
FREDERICK. You, niece. Within the next ten days, if you are found Within twenty miles of our public court, You die for it.

ROSALIND. I beg your Grace, Let me at least carry away knowledge of my offense. If I'm in touch with my own self, Or have any acquaintance with my own desires, If I'm not dreaming or out of my mind— And I trust I'm not—then, dear uncle, Not even by an unborn thought Have I offended your Highness.
FREDERICK. So all traitors talk. If their defense could be made in words, They'd be as innocent as grace itself. Let this be enough for you: I don't trust you.
ROSALIND. Yet your mistrust can't make me a traitor. Tell me, what is this suspicion based on?
FREDERICK. You are your father's daughter. That is enough.

ROSALIND. So I was when your Highness took his dukedom. So I was when your Highness banished him. Treason isn't inherited, my lord; And even if we did get it from our parents, What's that to me? My father was no traitor. So, my good lord, don't mistake me so much As to think my poverty is treacherous.
CELIA. Dear sovereign, hear me speak.
FREDERICK. Yes, Celia—we kept her here for your sake, Or else she would have gone wandering with her father.

CELIA. I didn't beg back then to have her stay; It was your pleasure and your own remorse. I was too young at the time to value her, But now I know her. If she's a traitor, Then so am I: we've always slept together, Risen at the same instant, learned, played, eaten together. And wherever we went, like Juno's swans, We went paired and inseparable.

FREDERICK. She is too clever for you; and her smoothness, Her very silence and her patience, Speak to the people, and they pity her. You are a fool. She robs you of your good name; And you'll shine brighter and seem more virtuous When she is gone. So don't open your lips. Firm and irrevocable is the doom I have passed on her: she is banished.
CELIA. Then pronounce that sentence on me too, my lord; I cannot live out of her company.
FREDERICK. You are a fool. You, niece—get yourself ready. If you overstay the time, on my honor, And on the weight of my word, you die. Exeunt DUKE and LORDS
CELIA. Oh my poor Rosalind! Where will you go? Will you change fathers? I'll give you mine. I beg you, don't be more grieved than I am.
ROSALIND. I have more reason to be.
CELIA. You do not, cousin. Please be cheerful. Don't you know the Duke Has banished me, his daughter?
ROSALIND. He hasn't.

CELIA. No, hasn't he? Then Rosalind lacks the love That teaches you that you and I are one. Shall we be sundered? Shall we part, sweet girl? No—let my father find another heir. So plan with me how we may flee, Where to go, and what to take with us; And don't try to take this burden on yourself, Bearing your griefs alone, and leaving me out; For, by this heaven now pale with our sorrows, Whatever you say, I'm going with you.
ROSALIND. Why, where shall we go?
CELIA. To seek my uncle in the Forest of Arden.
ROSALIND. Alas, what danger it will be for us, Maidens as we are, to travel so far! Beauty draws thieves sooner than gold.
CELIA. I'll put myself in poor and shabby clothes, And smudge my face with a kind of brown dye; You do the same. So we'll pass along And never attract attackers.

ROSALIND. Wouldn't it be better, Since I'm taller than the usual woman, That I dress in every detail like a man? A handsome cutlass at my thigh, A boar-spear in my hand—and in my heart, Whatever hidden woman's fear may lie— We'll wear a swaggering, martial outside, As many other mannish cowards do Who carry it off with appearances.
CELIA. What shall I call you when you're a man?
ROSALIND. I'll have no worse a name than Jove's own page, And therefore see that you call me Ganymede. But what will you be called?
CELIA. Something with a reference to my situation: No longer Celia, but Aliena.
ROSALIND. But, cousin, what if we tried to steal The clownish fool out of your father's court? Wouldn't he be a comfort on our travels?

CELIA. He'll come along over the wide world with me; Leave it to me to coax him. Let's go, And gather our jewels and our wealth together; Plan the fittest time and safest way To hide ourselves from the pursuit that will be made After my flight. Now we go in contentment To liberty, and not to banishment.                    Exeunt

ACT II. SCENE I. The Forest of Arden
Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, and two or three LORDS, like foresters

DUKE SENIOR. Now, my comrades and brothers in exile, Hasn't long custom made this life sweeter Than that of painted pomp? Aren't these woods More free from peril than the envious court? Here we don't feel Adam's punishment, The difference of the seasons—when the icy fang And churlish chiding of the winter wind Bite and blow upon my body, Even till I shrink with cold, I smile and say 'This is no flattery; these are counsellors That feelingly persuade me of what I am.' Sweet are the uses of adversity, Which, like the toad—ugly and venomous— Still wears a precious jewel in its head; And this life of ours, free from public haunt, Finds tongues in trees, books in running brooks, Sermons in stones, and good in everything. I would not change it.
AMIENS. Happy is your Grace, That can translate the stubbornness of fortune Into so quiet and so sweet a style.

DUKE SENIOR. Come, shall we go and kill some venison? And yet it pains me that the poor dappled creatures, Being native townsfolk of this wilderness city, Should, within their own bounds, with forked arrowheads Have their round haunches gored.

FIRST LORD. Indeed, my lord, The melancholy Jaques grieves at that; And on that score swears you usurp more Than your brother who has banished you. Today my Lord of Amiens and I Stole behind him as he lay stretched out Under an oak whose ancient root peeps out Over the brook that brawls along this wood! To that place a poor solitary stag, That from the hunter's aim had taken a wound, Came to languish; and indeed, my lord, The wretched animal heaved out such groans That their force stretched his leathery hide Almost to bursting; and the big round tears Coursed one after another down his innocent nose In piteous chase. And thus the hairy fool, Much watched by the melancholy Jaques, Stood on the extreme edge of the swift brook, Adding to it with his tears.
DUKE SENIOR. But what did Jaques say? Didn't he moralize this spectacle?

FIRST LORD. Oh yes, into a thousand similes. First, about the deer's weeping into the needless stream: 'Poor deer,' he said, 'you make a will Just as worldly people do, giving the bulk of your wealth To that which already has too much.' Then, being there alone, Left and abandoned by his velvet friends: ''Tis right,' said he, 'so misery parts The flow of company.' Soon afterward, a careless herd, Full from the pasture, jumps along past him And never stops to greet him. 'Yes,' said Jaques, 'Sweep on, you fat and greasy citizens; That's just the fashion. Why do you look At that poor and broken bankrupt there?' Thus most invectively he pierces through The body of the country, city, court, Yes, and of this life of ours; swearing that we Are mere usurpers, tyrants, and worse, To frighten the animals and kill them off In their assigned and native dwelling-place.
DUKE SENIOR. And did you leave him in this contemplation?
SECOND LORD. We did, my lord—weeping and commenting Upon the sobbing deer.
DUKE SENIOR. Show me the place. I love to engage him in these sullen moods, For then he's full of matter.
FIRST LORD. I'll bring you to him straight away.             Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2
paragraphs: The DUKE'S palace
Enter DUKE FREDERICK, with LORDS
FREDERICK. Can it possibly be that no one saw them? It can't be; some villains of my court Are in on this, by consent or by negligence.
FIRST LORD. I can't find anyone who saw her. The ladies who attend her in her chamber Saw her in bed, and early in the morning They found the bed empty of their mistress.

SECOND LORD. My lord, the scurvy clown, at whom your Grace So often used to laugh, is also missing. Hisperia, the Princess's gentlewoman, Confesses that she secretly overheard Your daughter and her cousin praising at length The qualities and graces of the wrestler Who only lately threw the sinewy Charles; And she believes, wherever they have gone, That youth is surely in their company.

FREDERICK. Send to his brother. Fetch that gallant here. If he is absent, bring his brother to me; I'll make him find him. Do this at once; And don't let the search and inquiry slacken Until you bring back these foolish runaways.                Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3
paragraphs: Before OLIVER'S house
Enter ORLANDO and ADAM, meeting
ORLANDO. Who's there?

ADAM. What, my young master? Oh, my gentle master! Oh, my sweet master! Oh, you remembrance Of old Sir Rowland! Why, what are you doing here? Why are you virtuous? Why do people love you? And why are you gentle, strong, and valiant? Why would you be so foolish as to overcome The handsome champion of the moody Duke? Your praise has reached home too swiftly before you. Don't you know, master, that for some kinds of men Their graces serve them only as enemies? So it is with yours. Your virtues, gentle master, Are sanctified and holy traitors to you. Oh, what a world it is, when what is fine Poisons the one who carries it!
ORLANDO. Why, what's the matter?

ADAM. Oh, unhappy young man! Don't come inside these doors; under this roof The enemy of all your graces lives. Your brother—no, no brother; yet the son— Yet not the son; I will not call him son Of the man I was about to call his father— Has heard your praises; and tonight he means To burn the lodging where you usually sleep, With you inside it. If he fails at that, He has other ways to cut you off. I overheard him and his schemes. This is no place for you; this house is just a slaughterhouse. Abhor it, fear it, do not enter it.
ORLANDO. Why, where, Adam, would you have me go?
ADAM. No matter where, so long as you don't come here.

ORLANDO. What, would you have me go and beg for my food, Or with a base and rough sword force A thievish living on the public road? That I must do, or I know not what to do; Yet that I will not do, however I can manage. I'd rather subject myself to the malice Of a degenerate and bloody brother.

ADAM. But don't do that. I have five hundred crowns, The thrifty wages I saved while under your father, Which I stored away to be my caregiver When my old limbs would no longer serve, And unregarded age was thrown into corners. Take it, and may He who feeds the ravens, Yes, providently caters for the sparrow, Be a comfort to my old age! Here is the gold; All of it I give to you. Let me be your servant. Though I look old, yet I am strong and lusty; For in my youth I never applied Hot and rebellious liquors to my blood, Nor with a shameless brow courted The means of weakness and debility. So my old age is like a hearty winter, Frosty, but kindly. Let me go with you; I'll do the work of a younger man In all your business and necessities.

ORLANDO. Oh, good old man, how well in you appears The steady service of the older world, When service sweated for duty, not for reward! You don't fit the fashion of these times, Where no one will sweat except for promotion, And once they have it, they choke off their service In the very having of it. It is not so with you. But, poor old man, you're pruning a rotten tree That can't produce so much as a blossom To repay all your pains and husbandry. But come along; we'll go together, And before we've spent your young man's wages We'll find some settled, modest contentment.

ADAM. Master, lead on; and I will follow you To the last gasp, with truth and loyalty. From seventeen years till now almost four-score I lived here, but now I live here no longer. At seventeen many seek their fortunes, But at fourscore it's too late in the week. Yet fortune can't reward me better Than to die well and not in my master's debt.          Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4
paragraphs: The Forest of Arden
Enter ROSALIND as GANYMEDE, CELIA as ALIENA, and CLOWN alias TOUCHSTONE
ROSALIND. Oh Jupiter, how weary my spirits are!
TOUCHSTONE. I wouldn't care about my spirits, if only my legs weren't weary.

ROSALIND. I could find it in my heart to disgrace my man's clothing and cry like a woman; but I must comfort the weaker vessel, since doublet and hose ought to show themselves courageous to petticoat. So, courage, good Aliena.
CELIA. Please, bear with me; I can't go any further.
TOUCHSTONE. For my part, I'd rather bear with you than carry you. Yet I'd be carrying no cross even if I did carry you, because I think you have no money in your purse.
ROSALIND. Well, this is the Forest of Arden.
TOUCHSTONE. Yes, now I'm in Arden—the bigger fool I. When I was at home, I was in a better place. But travelers must make do.
Enter CORIN and SILVIUS
ROSALIND. Yes, do that, good Touchstone. Look, who's coming—a young man and an old one in earnest talk.
CORIN. That's the way to make her go on scorning you.
SILVIUS. Oh Corin, if you only knew how I love her!
CORIN. I can partly guess; I've loved in my time too.

SILVIUS. No, Corin, being old, you can't guess, Though in your youth you were as true a lover As ever sighed upon a midnight pillow. But if your love was ever like mine— And I'm sure no man ever loved so— How many utterly ridiculous things Were you drawn into by your fancy?
CORIN. Into a thousand that I've forgotten.

SILVIUS. Oh, then you never loved so wholeheartedly! If you don't remember the slightest folly That love ever made you run into, You haven't loved. Or if you haven't sat as I do now, Wearing out your listener with your mistress's praises, You haven't loved. Or if you haven't broken from company Abruptly, the way my passion makes me now, You haven't loved. Oh Phebe, Phebe, Phebe!                          Exit Silvius
ROSALIND. Alas, poor shepherd! By searching out your wound, I've stumbled by accident on my own.

TOUCHSTONE. And I on mine. I remember when I was in love, I broke my sword on a stone and told it to take that for coming at night to Jane Smile. And I remember kissing her laundry-bat, and the cow's udders that her pretty chapped hands had milked. And I remember wooing a peapod instead of her—from which I took two pods, and giving them to her, said with tears, 'Wear these for my sake.' We who are true lovers run into strange capers; but as all is mortal in nature, so all of nature in love is mortal in folly.
ROSALIND. You speak more wisely than you realize.
TOUCHSTONE. No, I'll never be aware of my own wit until I break my shins against it.
ROSALIND. Jove, Jove! This shepherd's passion Looks very much like my own.
TOUCHSTONE. And mine—though it's growing somewhat stale with me.
CELIA. Please, one of you ask that man over there Whether he'll give us any food for gold; I'm fainting almost to death.
TOUCHSTONE. Hello there, you clown!
ROSALIND. Quiet, fool; he's not your kinsman.
CORIN. Who calls?
TOUCHSTONE. Your betters, sir.
CORIN. Otherwise they're very wretched indeed.
ROSALIND. Quiet, I say. Good evening to you, friend.
CORIN. And to you, gentle sir, and to you all.
ROSALIND. Please, shepherd, if love or gold Can buy a meal in this wild place, Bring us where we may rest and eat. Here's a young maid much oppressed by travel, And fainting for relief.

CORIN. Fair sir, I pity her, And wish, for her sake more than my own, My fortunes were more able to relieve her. But I'm shepherd to another man, And I don't shear the fleeces that I graze. My master is of churlish disposition, And cares little to find the way to heaven By doing deeds of hospitality. Besides, his cottage, his flocks, and his pastures Are now up for sale; and at our sheepcote now, Because of his absence, there's nothing You'd want to eat. But what there is, come see, And by my voice you'll be most welcome.
ROSALIND. Who is it that will buy his flock and pasture?
CORIN. That young swain you saw here just a moment ago, Who cares little for buying anything.
ROSALIND. Please, if it's honest to do so, You buy the cottage, pasture, and the flock, And we'll give you the money to pay for it.
CELIA. And we'll improve your wages. I like this place, And willingly could spend my time in it.

CORIN. Certainly the thing is up for sale. Come with me. If you like, after looking it over— The soil, the profit, and this kind of life— I'll be your very faithful steward, And buy it with your gold right away.             Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 5
paragraphs: Another part of the forest
Enter AMIENS, JAQUES, and OTHERS
SONG

AMIENS.    Under the greenwood tree Whoever loves to lie with me, And tune his merry note To the sweet bird's throat, Come hither, come hither, come hither. Here he shall see No enemy But winter and rough weather.
JAQUES. More, more, please, more.
AMIENS. It will make you melancholy, Monsieur Jaques.
JAQUES. I'm grateful for that. More, please, more. I can suck melancholy out of a song the way a weasel sucks eggs. More, please, more.
AMIENS. My voice is rough; I know I can't please you.
JAQUES. I don't want you to please me; I want you to sing. Come on, more—another stanza. Do you call them stanzas?
AMIENS. Whatever you wish, Monsieur Jaques.
JAQUES. No, I don't care what they're called; they owe me nothing. Will you sing?
AMIENS. More to oblige you than to please myself.

JAQUES. Well then, if I ever thank any man, I'll thank you. But what they call compliment is like the meeting of two baboons; and when a man thanks me heartily, it feels as if I've given him a penny and he's paying me back the beggarly thanks. Come on, sing—and those of you who won't, hold your tongues.
AMIENS. All right, I'll finish the song. Sirs, set the table meanwhile; the Duke will drink under this tree. He's been looking for you all day.
JAQUES. And I've been avoiding him all day. He's too argumentative for my company. I think about as many things as he does; but I thank heaven and don't boast about them. Come on, warble away.
SONG
[All together here]

Whoever shuns ambition, And loves to live in the sun, Seeking the food he eats, And pleased with what he gets, Come hither, come hither, come hither. Here he shall see No enemy But winter and rough weather.
JAQUES. I'll give you a verse for this tune that I made yesterday in spite of my own creativity.
AMIENS. And I'll sing it.
JAQUES. It goes like this:

If it should come to pass That any man turns ass, Leaving his wealth and ease A stubborn will to please, Ducdame, ducdame, ducdame; Here he shall see Gross fools just like he, If he'll come over to me.
AMIENS. What's that 'ducdame'?
JAQUES. It's a Greek invocation, to call fools into a circle. I'll go sleep, if I can; if I can't, I'll rant against all the first-born of Egypt.
AMIENS. And I'll go find the Duke; his banquet is ready. Exeunt severally

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 6
paragraphs: The forest
Enter ORLANDO and ADAM
ADAM. Dear master, I can't go any further. Oh, I'm dying for food! I'll lie down here and mark out my grave. Farewell, kind master.

ORLANDO. Why, what's this, Adam! No greater heart than that in you? Live a little; take a little comfort; cheer yourself a little. If this rough forest contains anything wild, I'll either be food for it or bring it back as food for you. Your imagination is nearer death than your strength is. For my sake, be brave; hold death off a little longer, at arm's length. I'll be back with you shortly; and if I don't bring you something to eat, I'll give you permission to die. But if you die before I come back, you're mocking my efforts. Well said! You're looking cheerful. I'll be with you quickly. But you're lying out in the bleak air. Come, I'll carry you to some shelter; and you shall not die for lack of a dinner, if anything alive exists in this wilderness. Cheer up, good Adam!          Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 7
paragraphs: The forest
A table set out. Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, and LORDS, like outlaws
DUKE SENIOR. I think he must have been transformed into a beast; For nowhere can I find him in the shape of a man.
FIRST LORD. My lord, he just now left this spot; He was here merrily, listening to a song.
DUKE SENIOR. If he, who's made of discord, grows musical, We'll soon have discord in the music of the spheres. Go find him; tell him I would speak with him.
Enter JAQUES
FIRST LORD. He saves me the trouble by coming on his own.
DUKE SENIOR. Why, what's this, monsieur! What kind of life is this, That your poor friends must beg for your company? What, you look merry!

JAQUES. A fool, a fool! I met a fool in the forest, A motley fool. A miserable world! As I live by food, I met a fool, Who laid himself down and basked in the sun, And railed at Lady Fortune in good terms, In well-formed terms—and yet a motley fool. 'Good morning, fool,' I said. 'No, sir,' he answered, 'Don't call me fool till heaven has sent me fortune.' And then he drew a sundial from his pouch, And, looking at it with a dull eye, Says very wisely, 'It is ten o'clock. Thus we may see,' he said, 'how the world wags. It's only an hour since it was nine; And after one hour more it will be eleven; And so, from hour to hour, we ripe and ripe, And then, from hour to hour, we rot and rot; And thereby hangs a tale.' When I heard The motley fool moralize like that on time, My lungs began to crow like a rooster That fools should be so deeply contemplative; And I laughed without stop For an hour by his dial. Oh, noble fool! A worthy fool! Motley is the only thing to wear.
DUKE SENIOR. What fool is this?

JAQUES. Oh, worthy fool! One who has been a courtier, And says that if ladies are only young and fair, They have the gift to know it. And in his brain, Which is as dry as the leftover biscuit After a voyage, he has strange places crammed With observation, which he gives out In mangled forms. Oh, that I were a fool! I'm ambitious for a motley coat.
DUKE SENIOR. You shall have one.

JAQUES. It is the only suit I want, Provided you weed your better judgments Of every opinion that has grown rank in them That I am wise. I must have liberty along with it— As large a charter as the wind, To blow on whom I please, for so fools do; And those who are most galled by my folly Must laugh the loudest. And why, sir, must they do so? The reason is plain as the path to the parish church: He whom a fool very wisely hits Acts very foolishly, although it stings him, Not to seem insensible of the blow. If he doesn't, The wise man's folly is anatomized Even by the random glances of the fool. Dress me in my motley; give me leave To speak my mind, and I will, through and through, Cleanse the foul body of this infected world, If they'll patiently receive my medicine.
DUKE SENIOR. Shame on you! I can tell what you'd do.
JAQUES. What, for a counter, would I do but good?

DUKE SENIOR. The most mischievous, foul sin of all—scolding sin. For you yourself have been a libertine, As sensual as the brutish sting itself; And all the swollen sores and headed evils That you with free license have caught, You would now disgorge into the wider world.

JAQUES. Why, who cries out against pride That can therein accuse any private person? Doesn't it flow as hugely as the sea, Till the wearer's very means ebb dry? What woman in the city do I name When I say the city-woman bears The cost of princes on unworthy shoulders? Who can come in and say I mean her, When her neighbor is just such another? Or what man of the basest occupation Is there, who says his finery isn't bought with my cost, Thinking I mean him, but in doing so fits His folly to the mettle of my speech? There then! How then? What then? Let me see how My tongue has wronged him: if it does him right, Then he has wronged himself; if he is innocent, Why, then my accusation flies like a wild goose, Claimed by no man. But who's coming here?
Enter ORLANDO with his sword drawn
ORLANDO. Stop, and eat no more.
JAQUES. Why, I haven't eaten any yet.
ORLANDO. Nor shall you, until necessity is served.
JAQUES. What kind of rooster does this one come from?
DUKE SENIOR. Are you made this bold, man, by your distress? Or are you a rude despiser of good manners, That you seem so empty of civility?

ORLANDO. You touched my vein at the first: the thorny point Of bare distress has stripped from me the show Of smooth civility. Yet I was brought up inland, And know some good breeding. But stop, I say; Anyone who touches any of this fruit dies Until I and my affairs are answered.
JAQUES. If you won't be answered with reason, then I must die.
DUKE SENIOR. What do you want? Your gentleness will compel More than your force will move us to gentleness.
ORLANDO. I'm almost dying for food, so let me have some.
DUKE SENIOR. Sit down and eat, and welcome to our table.

ORLANDO. Do you speak so gently? Pardon me, please; I thought all things here were savage, And so I put on the countenance Of stern command. But whoever you are That in this inaccessible wilderness, Under the shade of melancholy boughs, Lose and neglect the creeping hours of time; If you've ever known better days, If you've ever been where bells have rung for church, If you've ever sat at any good man's feast, If you've ever wiped a tear from your eyelid, And know what it is to pity and be pitied, Let gentleness be my strong enforcement; In hope of which I blush, and hide my sword.

DUKE SENIOR. It's true we've seen better days, And have been called to church by holy bell, And sat at good men's feasts, and wiped our eyes Of drops that sacred pity has engendered; And so sit down in gentleness, And take by request whatever help we have That can be ministered to your need.

ORLANDO. Then only hold back your food a little while, While, like a doe, I go to find my fawn, And give him food. There is an old poor man Who has, after me, in pure love Limped many a weary step. Till he is first satisfied, Oppressed by two weak evils, age and hunger, I will not touch a bite.
DUKE SENIOR. Go and find him. And we will waste nothing until you return.
ORLANDO. I thank you, and be blessed for your good comfort! Exit
DUKE SENIOR. You see we aren't alone in being unhappy: This wide and universal theater Presents more woeful pageants than the scene We play in.

JAQUES. All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players; They have their exits and their entrances, And one man in his time plays many parts, His acts being seven ages. At first the infant, Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms; Then the whining schoolboy, with his satchel And shining morning face, creeping like a snail Unwillingly to school. And then the lover, Sighing like a furnace, with a woeful ballad Made to his mistress's eyebrow. Then a soldier, Full of strange oaths and bearded like the leopard, Jealous in honor, sudden and quick to quarrel, Seeking the bubble reputation Even in the cannon's mouth. And then the justice, With fair round belly lined with good capon, With severe eyes and beard of formal cut, Full of wise sayings and modern examples; And so he plays his part. The sixth age shifts Into the lean and slippered pantaloon, With spectacles on his nose and pouch at his side; His youthful hose, well saved, a world too wide For his shrunken shank; and his big manly voice, Turning again toward childish treble, pipes And whistles in its sound. Last scene of all, That ends this strange eventful history, Is second childishness and mere oblivion— Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.
Re-enter ORLANDO with ADAM
DUKE SENIOR. Welcome. Set down your venerable burden, And let him eat.
ORLANDO. I thank you most on his behalf.
ADAM. As well you should; I can scarcely speak to thank you for myself.
DUKE SENIOR. Welcome; fall to. I won't trouble you As yet to ask about your fortunes. Give us some music; and, good cousin, sing.

SONG Blow, blow, you winter wind, You are not so unkind As man's ingratitude; Your tooth is not so keen, Because you are not seen, Although your breath be rough. Heigh-ho! sing heigh-ho! unto the green holly. Most friendship is feigning, most loving mere folly. Then, heigh-ho, the holly! This life is most jolly.
Freeze, freeze, you bitter sky, That do not bite so near As benefits forgot; Though you warp the waters, Your sting is not so sharp As a friend remembered not. Heigh-ho! sing, &c.

DUKE SENIOR. If you were the good Sir Rowland's son, As you have whispered faithfully you are, And as my eye does witness his likeness Most truly drawn and living in your face, Be truly welcome here. I am the Duke That loved your father. The rest of your story, Come to my cave and tell me. Good old man, You are right welcome, as your master is. Support him by the arm. Give me your hand, And let me understand all your fortunes.              Exeunt
ACT III. SCENE I. The palace
Enter DUKE FREDERICK, OLIVER, and LORDS

FREDERICK. Not seen him since! Sir, sir, that cannot be. But were I not made more of mercy than anything else, I wouldn't seek an absent target For my revenge while you are present. But see to it: Find out your brother wherever he is; Search him out with a candle; bring him back dead or living Within this twelvemonth, or never come back yourself To seek a living in our territory. Your lands and all things that you call yours Worth seizing we do seize into our hands, Until you can clear yourself by your brother's word Of what we think against you.
OLIVER. Oh, if only your Highness knew my heart in this! I never loved my brother in my life.

FREDERICK. The greater villain you. Well, push him out the doors; And let my officers of that kind Make an inventory of his house and lands. Do this with dispatch, and send him on his way.              Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2
paragraphs: The forest
Enter ORLANDO, with a paper

ORLANDO. Hang there, my verse, as witness of my love; And you, thrice-crowned Queen of the Night, survey With your chaste eye, from your pale sphere above, Your huntress's name that rules my whole life. O Rosalind! these trees shall be my books, And in their barks I'll inscribe my thoughts, So that every eye that looks in this forest Shall see your virtue witnessed everywhere. Run, run, Orlando; carve on every tree The fair, the chaste, the inexpressible she.             Exit
Enter CORIN and TOUCHSTONE
CORIN. And how do you like this shepherd's life, Master Touchstone?

TOUCHSTONE. Truly, shepherd, in itself it's a good life; but inasmuch as it is a shepherd's life, it is nothing. Inasmuch as it is solitary, I like it very well; but inasmuch as it is private, it's a very vile life. Now inasmuch as it's in the fields, it pleases me well; but inasmuch as it is not at court, it's tedious. As it is a simple life, you see, it suits my mood well; but as there is no more abundance in it, it goes much against my stomach. Have you any philosophy in you, shepherd?

CORIN. No more than that I know: the more sick a man is, the worse off he is; and that he who lacks money, means, and contentment lacks three good friends; that the property of rain is to wet, and fire to burn; that good pasture makes fat sheep; and that a great cause of night is lack of the sun; that he who has learned no wit by nature or by art may complain about his upbringing, or else he comes from very dull kin.
TOUCHSTONE. Such a one is a natural philosopher. Have you ever been at court, shepherd?
CORIN. No, truly.
TOUCHSTONE. Then you are damned.
CORIN. No, I hope not.
TOUCHSTONE. Truly, you are damned, like an ill-roasted egg, all on one side.
CORIN. For not being at court? Give me your reason.

TOUCHSTONE. Why, if you were never at court, you never saw good manners; if you never saw good manners, then your manners must be wicked; and wickedness is sin, and sin is damnation. You're in a perilous state, shepherd.

CORIN. Not a bit, Touchstone. Those things that count as good manners at court are as ridiculous in the country as the behavior of the country is most mockable at court. You told me that at court you don't bow but kiss your hands. That kind of courtesy would be unclean if courtiers were shepherds.
TOUCHSTONE. An example, briefly; come, an example.
CORIN. Well, we are always handling our ewes, and their fleeces, you know, are greasy.
TOUCHSTONE. Why, don't courtiers' hands sweat? And isn't the grease of a sheep as wholesome as the sweat of a man? Shallow, shallow. A better example, I say; come on.
CORIN. Besides, our hands are hard.
TOUCHSTONE. Your lips will feel them all the sooner. Shallow again. A sounder example; come.
CORIN. And they are often tarred over from doctoring our sheep; and would you have us kiss tar? Courtiers' hands are perfumed with civet.

TOUCHSTONE. Most shallow man! You're worm's-meat compared to a good piece of flesh, indeed! Learn from the wise, and consider: civet is of a baser birth than tar—the very uncleanly discharge of a cat. Improve your example, shepherd.
CORIN. You have too courtly a wit for me; I'll give up.
TOUCHSTONE. Will you give up and be damned? God help you, shallow man! God make an incision in you! You are raw.

CORIN. Sir, I am a true laborer: I earn what I eat, get what I wear; owe no man hate, envy no man's happiness; glad of other men's good, content with my own harm; and the greatest pride I have is to see my ewes graze and my lambs suck.

TOUCHSTONE. That is another simple sin in you: to bring the ewes and the rams together, and to make your living by the copulation of livestock; to be pimp to a bellwether, and to betray a year-old female lamb to a crooked-headed, old, cuckoldly ram, totally unsuited to her. If you aren't damned for this, the devil himself will have no shepherds; I can't see otherwise how you can escape.
CORIN. Here comes young Master Ganymede, my new mistress's brother.
Enter ROSALIND, reading a paper

ROSALIND.   'From the east to the western Indies, No jewel is like Rosalind. Her worth, being carried on the wind, Through all the world bears the name of Rosalind. All the pictures most beautifully drawn Are but dark beside Rosalind. Let no face be kept in mind But the fairness of Rosalind.'
TOUCHSTONE. I could rhyme you like that for eight years straight, leaving out only dinners, suppers, and sleeping hours. It's the regular butter-women's plodding rhythm to market.
ROSALIND. Get out, fool!

TOUCHSTONE.   For a sample: If a hart should lack a hind, Let him seek out Rosalind. If the cat will mate in kind, So as surely will Rosalind. Winter garments must be lined, So must slender Rosalind. They that reap must sheaf and bind, Then to cart with Rosalind. Sweetest nut has sourest rind, Such a nut is Rosalind. He that the sweetest rose will find Must find love's thorn and Rosalind. This is the very false gallop of verses; why are you infecting yourself with them?
ROSALIND. Quiet, you dull fool! I found them on a tree.
TOUCHSTONE. Truly, the tree yields bad fruit.

ROSALIND. I'll graft it with you, and then I'll graft it with a medlar. Then it will produce the earliest fruit in the country; for you'll be rotten before you're half ripe, and that's the special quality of the medlar.
TOUCHSTONE. You have spoken; but whether wisely or not, let the forest judge.
Enter CELIA, with a writing
ROSALIND. Quiet! Here comes my sister, reading; stand aside.

CELIA.   'Why should this be a desert? Because it is unpeopled? No; I'll hang tongues on every tree That shall reveal civil sayings. Some, about how brief the life of man Runs his erring pilgrimage, And that the stretch of a hand-span Buckles in the sum of his age; Some, about violated vows Between the souls of friend and friend; But upon the fairest boughs, Or at every sentence end, I will write 'Rosalinda,' Teaching all who read to know The quintessence of every spirit That heaven would in little show. Therefore heaven charged Nature That one body should be filled With all graces widely spread. Nature immediately distilled Helen's cheek, but not her heart, Cleopatra's majesty, Atalanta's better part, Sad Lucretia's modesty. Thus Rosalind of many parts By heavenly synod was devised, Of many faces, eyes, and hearts, To have the touches most dearly prized. Heaven willed that she should have these gifts, And I, to live and die her slave.'
ROSALIND. O most gentle Jupiter! What a tedious sermon of love you've wearied your parishioners with—and never cried 'Have patience, good people.'
CELIA. What now! Back, friends—shepherd, step off a bit; go with him, sirrah.
TOUCHSTONE. Come, shepherd, let us make an honorable retreat;
though not with bag and baggage, yet with knapsack and contents. Exeunt CORIN and TOUCHSTONE
CELIA. Did you hear those verses?
ROSALIND. Oh yes, I heard them all, and more besides—because some of them had more feet than the verses could bear.
CELIA. That's no matter; the feet might bear up the verses.
ROSALIND. Yes, but the feet were lame, and couldn't bear themselves without the verse, and so they stood lamely in the verse.
CELIA. But did you hear without wondering how your name comes to be hanging and carved upon these trees?

ROSALIND. I was seven of the nine days out of wondering before you came; for look here what I found on a palm-tree. I haven't been so rhymed at since Pythagoras' time, when I was an Irish rat—which I can hardly remember.
CELIA. Can you guess who has done this?
ROSALIND. Is it a man?
CELIA. And with a chain about his neck that you once wore. Are you changing color?
ROSALIND. Please, who?
CELIA. O Lord, Lord! It's a hard thing for friends to meet; but mountains may be moved by earthquakes, and so encounter each other.
ROSALIND. No, but who is it?
CELIA. Is it possible?
ROSALIND. No, please, now, with the most petitionary vehemence, tell me who it is.
CELIA. Oh wonderful, wonderful, most wonderful wonderful, and yet again wonderful, and beyond all whooping!

ROSALIND. Mercy on my complexion! Do you think, just because I'm dressed up like a man, I have a doublet and hose in my temperament too? One inch more of delay is a South Sea of discovery. Please tell me who it is, quickly, and speak fast. I wish you could stammer, so you could pour this concealed man out of your mouth, as wine comes out of a narrow-mouthed bottle—either too much at once or none at all. Please, take the cork out of your mouth so I can drink your tidings.
CELIA. So you can put a man inside your belly.
ROSALIND. Is he of God's making? What kind of man? Is his head worth a hat or his chin worth a beard?
CELIA. No, he has only a little beard.
ROSALIND. Why, God will send more if the man will be thankful. I'll wait for his beard to grow, so long as you don't make me wait for the news of his chin.
CELIA. It is young Orlando, who tripped up the wrestler's heels and your heart both in the same instant.
ROSALIND. No, but the devil take mocking! Speak with a serious brow and as a truthful maid.
CELIA. In faith, cousin, it's him.
ROSALIND. Orlando?
CELIA. Orlando.

ROSALIND. Alas the day! What shall I do with my doublet and hose? What was he doing when you saw him? What did he say? How did he look? What was he wearing? What's he doing here? Did he ask for me? Where's he staying? How did he take leave of you? And when will you see him again? Answer me in one word.
CELIA. First you must lend me Gargantua's mouth; that's a word too big for any mouth of this age's size. To say yes and no to all these particulars is more than answering a catechism.
ROSALIND. But does he know that I am in this forest, and in man's clothing? Does he look as fresh as he did the day he wrestled?
CELIA. It's as easy to count motes of dust as to settle the questions of a lover. But have a taste of how I found him, and savor it with attention. I found him under a tree, like a dropped acorn.
ROSALIND. It may well be called Jove's tree, when it drops such fruit.
CELIA. Hear me out, good madam.
ROSALIND. Proceed.
CELIA. There he lay, stretched out like a wounded knight.
ROSALIND. Though it's a pity to see such a sight, it suits the ground well.
CELIA. Cry 'Whoa' to your tongue, please; it's prancing out of season. He was outfitted like a hunter.
ROSALIND. Oh, ominous! He comes to kill my heart.
CELIA. I'd like to sing my song without an interruption; you're throwing me off-key.
ROSALIND. Don't you know I am a woman? When I think, I must speak. Sweet, go on.
CELIA. You're putting me off. Soft! Isn't that him coming here?
Enter ORLANDO and JAQUES
ROSALIND. It's him. Slink by, and watch him.
JAQUES. I thank you for your company; but in good faith, I'd just as soon have been alone.
ORLANDO. And so would I; but yet, for fashion's sake, I thank you also for your company.
JAQUES. God be with you; let's meet as little as we can.
ORLANDO. I do wish we may be better strangers.
JAQUES. Please, mar no more trees by writing love songs in their barks.
ORLANDO. Please, mar no more of my verses by reading them so badly.
JAQUES. Rosalind is your love's name?
ORLANDO. Yes, just so.
JAQUES. I don't like her name.
ORLANDO. There was no thought of pleasing you when she was christened.
JAQUES. What height is she?
ORLANDO. Just as high as my heart.
JAQUES. You are full of pretty answers. Haven't you been hanging around with goldsmiths' wives, and memorized them off rings?
ORLANDO. Not so; rather, I answer you straight from painted cloth, from which you have studied your questions.
JAQUES. You have a nimble wit; I think it was made from Atalanta's heels. Will you sit down with me? And we two will rail against our mistress the world, and all our misery.
ORLANDO. I will scold no living creature in the world but myself, against whom I know the most faults.
JAQUES. The worst fault you have is being in love.
ORLANDO. That's a fault I would not exchange for your best virtue. I'm weary of you.
JAQUES. By my faith, I was looking for a fool when I found you.
ORLANDO. He's drowned in the brook; just look in, and you'll see him.
JAQUES. There I shall see my own figure.
ORLANDO. Which I take to be either a fool or a zero.
JAQUES. I'll stay no longer with you. Farewell, good Signior Love.
ORLANDO. I'm glad of your departure; adieu, good Monsieur Melancholy. Exit JAQUES
ROSALIND. [Aside to CELIA] I'll speak to him like a saucy lackey, and under that disguise play the knave with him.—Do you hear, forester?
ORLANDO. Very well; what do you want?
ROSALIND. Please, what time is it?
ORLANDO. You should ask me what time of day it is; there's no clock in the forest.
ROSALIND. Then there's no true lover in the forest, since sighing every minute and groaning every hour would detect the lazy foot of Time as well as a clock.
ORLANDO. And why not the swift foot of Time? Wouldn't that have been as proper?
ROSALIND. By no means, sir. Time travels at different paces with different people. I'll tell you with whom Time ambles, with whom Time trots, with whom Time gallops, and with whom he stands still.
ORLANDO. Please, with whom does he trot?

ROSALIND. Why, he trots hard with a young maid between the contract of her marriage and the day it is solemnized. If the interval is only a week, Time's pace is so hard that it seems the length of seven years.
ORLANDO. With whom does Time amble?

ROSALIND. With a priest who lacks Latin and a rich man who hasn't got the gout; the one sleeps easily because he can't study, and the other lives merrily because he feels no pain; the one lacking the burden of lean and wasteful learning, the other knowing no burden of heavy tedious poverty. With these two Time ambles.
ORLANDO. With whom does he gallop?
ROSALIND. With a thief on his way to the gallows; for though he goes as softly as foot can fall, he thinks himself there too soon.
ORLANDO. With whom does he stand still?
ROSALIND. With lawyers during the vacation; for they sleep between term and term, and so they don't perceive how Time moves.
ORLANDO. Where do you live, pretty youth?
ROSALIND. With this shepherdess, my sister; here on the outskirts of the forest, like fringe on a petticoat.
ORLANDO. Are you native to this place?
ROSALIND. As is the rabbit that you see live where she's born.
ROSALIND. Your accent is somewhat finer than you could have acquired in such a remote dwelling.

ROSALIND. So I have been told by many; but indeed, an old religious uncle of mine taught me to speak. He was in his youth an inland man—one who knew courtship too well, for there he fell in love. I've heard him read many lectures against it; and I thank God I am not a woman, to be tainted with so many giddy offenses as he generally charged their whole sex with.
ORLANDO. Can you remember any of the principal evils he laid to women's charge?
ROSALIND. There were no principal ones; they were all like one another the way halfpennies are; every fault seemed monstrous till its fellow-fault came along to match it.
ORLANDO. Please recount some of them.

ROSALIND. No; I won't waste my medicine on any but the sick. There's a man who haunts the forest abusing our young plants by carving 'Rosalind' on their barks; hanging odes upon hawthorns and elegies on brambles—all, indeed, deifying the name of Rosalind. If I could meet that fancy-monger, I'd give him some good counsel, for he seems to have the daily fever of love upon him.
ORLANDO. I am the one so love-shaken; please tell me your remedy.
ROSALIND. There's none of my uncle's marks upon you; he taught me how to recognize a man in love; and you, I'm sure, are not a prisoner in that cage of rushes.
ORLANDO. What were his marks?

ROSALIND. A lean cheek, which you don't have; a blue, sunken eye, which you don't have; an unquestionable spirit, which you don't have; a neglected beard, which you don't have—but I pardon you for that, since what little beard you have is a younger brother's revenue. Then your hose should be ungartered, your bonnet without a band, your sleeve unbuttoned, your shoe untied, and everything about you showing a careless desolation. But you are no such man; you're rather point-perfect in your dress, looking like a lover of yourself rather than a lover of anyone else.
ORLANDO. Fair youth, I wish I could make you believe I am in love.

ROSALIND. Me believe it! You may as soon make her that you love believe it; which, I assure you, she's quicker to do than to confess she does. That's one of the points on which women still give the lie to their consciences. But, truly now, are you the one who hangs the verses on the trees in which Rosalind is so admired?
ORLANDO. I swear to you, youth, by the white hand of Rosalind, I am he—that unfortunate he.
ROSALIND. But are you really as much in love as your rhymes say?
ORLANDO. Neither rhyme nor reason can express how much.

ROSALIND. Love is merely a madness; and, I tell you, it deserves a dark house and a whip as much as madmen do. The reason they aren't so punished and cured is that the lunacy is so common that the whippers are in love too. Yet I claim to cure it by counsel.
ORLANDO. Did you ever cure any so?

ROSALIND. Yes, one; and in this way. He was to imagine me his love, his mistress; and I set him every day to woo me. At which times I, being but a moonish youth, would grieve, be effeminate, changeable, longing and liking, proud, fantastical, apish, shallow, inconstant, full of tears, full of smiles—for every passion something, and for no passion truly anything, as boys and women are for the most part creatures of this stripe. I'd now like him, now loathe him; then entertain him, then forswear him; now weep for him, then spit at him—so I drove my suitor from his mad humor of love into a living humor of madness, which was to forswear the full stream of the world and to live in a corner merely monastic. And thus I cured him; and this way I'll undertake to wash your liver as clean as a sound sheep's heart, so there shall not be one spot of love in it.
ORLANDO. I would not be cured, youth.
ROSALIND. I would cure you, if you would just call me Rosalind, and come every day to my cottage and woo me.
ORLANDO. Now, by the faith of my love, I will. Tell me where it is.
ROSALIND. Come with me to it, and I'll show you; and on the way, you can tell me where in the forest you live. Will you come?
ORLANDO. With all my heart, good youth.
ROSALIND. No, you must call me Rosalind. Come, sister, will you come?                                                   Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3
paragraphs: The forest
Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY; JAQUES behind
TOUCHSTONE. Come along quickly, good Audrey; I'll fetch up your goats, Audrey. And how about it, Audrey—am I the man yet? Does my simple appearance content you?
AUDREY. Your features! Lord protect us! What features?
TOUCHSTONE. I am here with you and your goats, just as the most capricious poet, honest Ovid, was among the Goths.
JAQUES. [Aside] Oh, knowledge poorly housed, worse than Jove in a thatched cottage!

TOUCHSTONE. When a man's verses can't be understood, nor a man's good wit backed up by the forward child Understanding, it strikes a man deader than a great bill in a little room. Truly, I wish the gods had made you poetical.
AUDREY. I don't know what 'poetical' is. Is it honest in deed and word? Is it a true thing?
TOUCHSTONE. No, truly; the truest poetry is the most feigning, and lovers are given to poetry; and what they swear in poetry may be said, as lovers, they only feign.
AUDREY. Do you wish, then, that the gods had made me poetical?
TOUCHSTONE. I do, truly, because you swear to me you are honest. Now, if you were a poet, I might have some hope you were faking.
AUDREY. Wouldn't you have me honest?
TOUCHSTONE. No, truly, unless you were ugly. For honesty coupled with beauty is like having honey as a sauce for sugar.
JAQUES. [Aside] A substantial fool!
AUDREY. Well, I'm not pretty; and so I pray the gods to make me honest.
TOUCHSTONE. Truly, and to throw away honesty on a foul slut would be to put good meat into an unclean dish.
AUDREY. I am not a slut, though I thank the gods I am foul.

TOUCHSTONE. Well, praised be the gods for your foulness; sluttishness may come hereafter. But be it as it may, I'll marry you. And to that end I have been with Sir Oliver Martext, the vicar of the next village, who has promised to meet me here in this place in the forest and join us together.
JAQUES. [Aside] I'd love to see this meeting.
AUDREY. Well, may the gods give us joy!

TOUCHSTONE. Amen. A man might, if he had a fearful heart, hesitate at this attempt; for here we have no temple but the wood, no assembly but horned beasts. But what of it? Courage! As horns are odious, they are necessary. It is said: 'Many a man knows no end of his goods.' Right! Many a man has good horns and knows no end of them. Well, those are his wife's dowry; they're none of his own getting. Horns? Just so. Only on poor men? No, no; the noblest deer has them as huge as the rascal. Is the single man therefore blessed? No; as a walled town is more worthy than a village, so is the forehead of a married man more honorable than the bare brow of a bachelor. And by as much as defense is better than no skill, by so much is having a horn more precious than to lack one. Here comes Sir Oliver.
Enter SIR OLIVER MARTEXT
Sir Oliver Martext, well met. Will you dispatch us here under this tree, or shall we go with you to your chapel?
MARTEXT. Is there no one here to give the woman away?
TOUCHSTONE. I won't take her as a gift from any man.
MARTEXT. Truly, she must be given away, or the marriage isn't lawful.
JAQUES. [Discovering himself] Proceed, proceed; I'll give her away.

TOUCHSTONE. Good evening, good Master What-do-you-call-him; how are you, sir? You're well met. God reward you for your last company. I'm very glad to see you. Just a trifle in hand here, sir. No; please, keep your hat on.
JAQUES. Will you be married, motley?
TOUCHSTONE. As the ox has his yoke, sir, the horse his curb, and the falcon her bells, so man has his desires; and as pigeons bill, so wedlock would be nibbling.

JAQUES. And will you, being a man of your breeding, be married under a bush, like a beggar? Get yourself to a church and find a good priest who can tell you what marriage is. This fellow will only join you together as they join wainscot; then one of you will prove to be a shrunk panel, and like green timber, warp, warp.

TOUCHSTONE. [Aside] I'm of a mind that I'm better off married by him than by another. He's not likely to marry me well, and not being well married will be a good excuse for me hereafter to leave my wife.
JAQUES. Come along with me, and let me counsel you.

TOUCHSTONE. Come, sweet Audrey; We must be married, or we must live in vice. Farewell, good Master Oliver. Not— O sweet Oliver, O brave Oliver, Leave me not behind you. But— Be off, Begone, I say, I will not go to wedding with you. Exeunt JAQUES, TOUCHSTONE, and AUDREY
MARTEXT. No matter; not one fantastical knave among them all shall mock me out of my calling.                       Exit

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4
paragraphs: The forest
Enter ROSALIND and CELIA
ROSALIND. Don't talk to me; I'm going to weep.
CELIA. Do, please; but yet have the grace to consider that tears don't become a man.
ROSALIND. But haven't I cause to weep?
CELIA. As good a cause as anyone could want; so weep.
ROSALIND. His very hair is of the deceiving color.
CELIA. Something browner than Judas's. Marry, his kisses are Judas's own children.
ROSALIND. By my faith, his hair is of a good color.
CELIA. An excellent color: your chestnut was always the only color.
ROSALIND. And his kissing is as full of sanctity as the touch of holy bread.
CELIA. He has bought a pair of cast-off lips from Diana. A nun of the winter sisterhood doesn't kiss more religiously; the very ice of chastity is in them.
ROSALIND. But why did he swear he would come this morning, and isn't here?
CELIA. No, certainly, there is no truth in him.
ROSALIND. Do you think so?
CELIA. Yes; I think he's not a pickpurse or a horse-thief; but for his truthfulness in love, I think him as hollow as a covered goblet or a worm-eaten nut.
ROSALIND. Not true in love?
CELIA. Yes, when he is in love; but I don't think he's in.
ROSALIND. You heard him swear flat out that he was.

CELIA. 'Was' is not 'is'; besides, the oath of a lover is no stronger than the word of a tavern-keeper; they're both confirmers of false reckonings. He attends here in the forest on the Duke, your father.

ROSALIND. I met the Duke yesterday, and had much conversation with him. He asked me of what parentage I was. I told him, of as good as his; so he laughed and let me go. But what are we talking about fathers for, when there's such a man as Orlando?

CELIA. Oh, that's a brave man! He writes brave verses, speaks brave words, swears brave oaths, and breaks them bravely—quite athwart, sideways across the heart of his lover; like a puny jouster who spurs his horse on only one side, and breaks his staff like a noble goose. But all things are brave that youth mounts and folly guides. Who's coming here?
Enter CORIN

CORIN. Mistress and master, you have often inquired After the shepherd who complained of love, Whom you saw sitting by me on the turf, Praising the proud and disdainful shepherdess Who was his mistress.
CELIA. Well, and what of him?

CORIN. If you would like to see a pageant truly played Between the pale complexion of true love And the red glow of scorn and proud disdain, Come a little way from here, and I'll conduct you, If you'd like to observe.
ROSALIND. Oh, come, let's go! The sight of lovers feeds those who are in love. Bring us to this sight, and you'll say I'll play a busy actor in their play.                Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 5
paragraphs: Another part of the forest
Enter SILVIUS and PHEBE

SILVIUS. Sweet Phebe, do not scorn me; do not, Phebe. Say that you do not love me; but do not say it In bitterness. The common executioner, Whose heart the accustomed sight of death makes hard, Does not let the axe fall upon the humbled neck Without first begging pardon. Will you be sterner Than he who lives and dies by bloody drops?
Enter ROSALIND, CELIA, and CORIN, at a distance

PHEBE. I would not be your executioner; I flee from you, because I would not injure you. You tell me there is murder in my eye. That's a pretty notion, surely, and very probable, That eyes—which are the most fragile and softest things, Which shut their cowardly gates against motes of dust— Should be called tyrants, butchers, murderers! Now I do frown on you with all my heart; And if my eyes can wound, now let them kill you. Now pretend to swoon; why, now fall down; Or if you cannot, oh, for shame, for shame, Do not lie and say my eyes are murderers. Now show me the wound my eye has made in you. Scratch yourself with a pin and there remains Some scar of it; lean upon a rush, And the imprint and visible impression Your palm keeps for a moment; but now my eyes, Which I have darted at you, hurt you not; Nor, I am sure, is there force in eyes That can do hurt.
SILVIUS. Oh dear Phebe, If ever—and that may be near at hand— You meet in some fresh cheek the power of love, Then you shall know the wounds invisible That love's keen arrows make.
PHEBE. But till that time Don't come near me; and when that time comes, Afflict me with your mockery, do not pity me; As until that time, I shall not pity you.

ROSALIND. [Advancing] And why, please tell me? Who might be your mother, That you insult, exult, and all at once, Over the wretched? What though you have no beauty— For, by my faith, I see no more in you Than someone might see going to bed in the dark without a candle— Must you therefore be proud and pitiless? Why, what does this mean? Why do you look at me? I see no more in you than in the ordinary Sale-work of nature. By my life, I think she means to tangle my eyes too! No, faith, proud mistress, don't hope for it; It is not your inky brows, your black silk hair, Your bead-like eyeballs, nor your cheek of cream That can tame my spirit into worshiping you. You foolish shepherd, why do you follow her, Like the foggy south, puffing with wind and rain? You are a thousand times more proper a man Than she is a woman. It is such fools as you That make the world full of ill-favored children. It is not her mirror, but you, that flatters her; And out of you she sees herself more proper Than any of her features can show her. But, mistress, know yourself. Down on your knees, And thank heaven, fasting, for a good man's love; For I must tell you, friendly in your ear: Sell when you can; you are not for all markets. Beg the man's mercy, love him, take his offer; Foul is most foul, being foul, to be a scoffer. So, take her to yourself, shepherd. Fare you well.
PHEBE. Sweet youth, please, scold me for a whole year together; I'd rather hear you chide than hear this man woo.

ROSALIND. He's fallen in love with your foulness, and she'll fall in love with my anger. If so, as fast as she answers you with frowning looks, I'll season her with bitter words. Why do you look so at me?
PHEBE. For no ill will I bear you.

ROSALIND. Please don't fall in love with me, For I am falser than vows made in wine; Besides, I do not like you. If you want to know where I live, It's at the tuft of olive trees nearby. Will you come, sister? Shepherd, press her hard. Come, sister. Shepherdess, look on him more kindly, And be not proud; though all the world could see, None could be so deceived in sight as he. Come, to our flock.        Exeunt ROSALIND, CELIA, and CORIN
PHEBE. Dead shepherd, now I find your saying of might: 'Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?'
SILVIUS. Sweet Phebe.
PHEBE. Ha! What do you say, Silvius?
SILVIUS. Sweet Phebe, pity me.
PHEBE. Why, I am sorry for you, gentle Silvius.
SILVIUS. Wherever sorrow is, relief should be. If you sorrow at my grief in love, By giving love, your sorrow and my grief Would both be ended.
PHEBE. You have my love; isn't that neighborly?
SILVIUS. I want to have you.

PHEBE. Why, that would be covetousness. Silvius, there was a time when I hated you; And yet it is not that I bear you love now; But since you can talk of love so well, Your company, which used to be irksome to me, I will endure; and I'll employ you too. But don't look for further reward Than your own gladness that you're employed.

SILVIUS. So holy and so perfect is my love, And I in such a poverty of grace, That I shall think it a most plenteous crop To glean the broken ears of grain behind the man Who reaps the main harvest; if I might gather, now and then, A scattered smile, I would live upon that.
PHEBE. Do you know the youth that spoke to me a while ago?
SILVIUS. Not very well; but I've met him often; And he has bought the cottage and the lands That the old peasant once was master of.

PHEBE. Don't think I love him, though I ask about him; He's only a peevish boy; yet he talks well. But what care I for words? Yet words do well When he that speaks them pleases those who hear. He is a pretty youth—not very pretty; But, sure, he's proud; and yet his pride becomes him. He'll make a proper man. The best thing in him Is his complexion; and faster than his tongue Did offense, his eye healed it up. He's not very tall; yet for his years he's tall; His leg is only so-so; and yet it's well enough. There was a pretty redness in his lip, A little riper and more lusty red Than the red mixed in his cheek; it was just the difference Between the constant red and the mingled damask. There are some women, Silvius—had they marked him In parts as I did—would have come close To falling in love with him; but, for my part, I love him not, nor hate him not; and yet I have more cause to hate him than to love him; For what did he have to do, to chide at me? He said my eyes were black, and my hair black, And, now I remember, scorned at me. I wonder why I didn't answer him back; But that's all one: silence is no surrender. I'll write him a very taunting letter, And you shall carry it; will you, Silvius?
SILVIUS. Phebe, with all my heart.
PHEBE. I'll write it straight away. The matter's in my head and in my heart; I will be bitter with him, and exceedingly brief. Go with me, Silvius.                                  Exeunt
