ACT IV. SCENE I. The forest
Enter ROSALIND, CELIA, and JAQUES
JAQUES. Please, pretty youth, let me become better acquainted with you.
ROSALIND. They say you are a melancholy fellow.
JAQUES. I am; I like it better than laughing.
ROSALIND. Those who are in extremes of either are abominable fellows, and betray themselves to every modern censure worse than drunkards do.
JAQUES. Why, it's good to be sad and say nothing.
ROSALIND. Why then, it's good to be a fence-post.

JAQUES. I have neither the scholar's melancholy, which is rivalry; nor the musician's, which is fantastical; nor the courtier's, which is proud; nor the soldier's, which is ambitious; nor the lawyer's, which is calculating; nor the lady's, which is fastidious; nor the lover's, which is all of these; but it is a melancholy of my own, compounded of many simples, extracted from many objects, and indeed the various contemplation of my travels; in which my frequent rumination wraps me in a most humorous sadness.

ROSALIND. A traveler! By my faith, you have great reason to be sad. I fear you've sold your own lands to see other men's; then to have seen much and to have nothing is to have rich eyes and poor hands.
JAQUES. Yes, I have gained my experience.
Enter ORLANDO
ROSALIND. And your experience makes you sad. I'd rather have a fool to make me merry than experience to make me sad—and to travel to get it, too.
ORLANDO. Good day, and happiness, dear Rosalind!
JAQUES. No, then, God be with you, since you talk in blank verse.

ROSALIND. Farewell, Monsieur Traveler; mind you lisp and wear strange suits, disparage all the benefits of your own country, be out of love with your nativity, and almost scold God for making you that face you have; or I'll scarcely believe you have swum in a gondola. [Exit JAQUES] Why, what now, Orlando! Where have you been all this while? You, a lover! If you serve me such another trick, never come into my sight again.
ORLANDO. My fair Rosalind, I come within an hour of my promise.

ROSALIND. Break an hour's promise in love! He who will divide a minute into a thousand parts, and break only a part of the thousand part of a minute in the affairs of love, it may be said of him that Cupid has clapped him on the shoulder, but I'll guarantee him heart-whole.
ORLANDO. Pardon me, dear Rosalind.
ROSALIND. No, if you are so tardy, come no more in my sight. I'd just as soon be wooed by a snail.
ORLANDO. By a snail!
ROSALIND. Yes, by a snail; for though he comes slowly, he carries his house on his head—a better jointure-settlement, I think, than you make for a woman. Besides, he brings his destiny with him.
ORLANDO. What's that?
ROSALIND. Why, horns—the kind that men like you are bound to be indebted to your wives for; but he comes armed in his own fortune, and prevents the slander of his wife.
ORLANDO. Virtue is no horn-maker; and my Rosalind is virtuous.
ROSALIND. And I am your Rosalind.
CELIA. It pleases him to call you so; but he has a Rosalind of a better look than you.
ROSALIND. Come, woo me, woo me; for now I am in a holiday mood, and likely enough to consent. What would you say to me now, if I were your very, very Rosalind?
ORLANDO. I would kiss before I spoke.

ROSALIND. No, you'd better speak first; and when you were stuck for lack of matter, you might take occasion to kiss. Very good orators, when they run dry, will spit; and for lovers lacking—God help us!—matter, the cleanliest shift is to kiss.
ORLANDO. What if the kiss is denied?
ROSALIND. Then she puts you to entreaty, and there begins new matter.
ORLANDO. Who could run out of words, being before his beloved mistress?
ROSALIND. Marry, you would, if I were your mistress; or I should think my honesty stronger than my wit.
ORLANDO. What, out of my suit?
ROSALIND. Not out of your apparel, and yet out of your suit. Am I not your Rosalind?
ORLANDO. I take some joy in saying you are, because I'd like to be talking of her.
ROSALIND. Well, in her person, I say I will not have you.
ORLANDO. Then, in my own person, I die.

ROSALIND. No, faith, die by proxy. The poor world is almost six thousand years old, and in all that time there was never any man who died in his own person, that is to say, from love. Troilus had his brains dashed out with a Grecian club; yet he did what he could to die before, and he is one of the patterns of love. Leander would have lived many a fair year, even if Hero had turned nun, if it hadn't been for a hot midsummer night; for, good youth, he only went out to wash himself in the Hellespont, and, being seized by a cramp, was drowned; and the foolish chroniclers of that age said it was for love of Hero of Sestos. But these are all lies: men have died from time to time, and worms have eaten them, but not for love.
ORLANDO. I wouldn't have my true Rosalind think this way; for I swear, her frown might kill me.
ROSALIND. By this hand, it wouldn't kill a fly. But come, now I'll be your Rosalind in a more accommodating mood; and ask me what you will, I'll grant it.
ORLANDO. Then love me, Rosalind.
ROSALIND. Yes, faith, I will, Fridays and Saturdays, and all.
ORLANDO. And will you have me?
ROSALIND. Yes, and twenty such.
ORLANDO. What do you say?
ROSALIND. Aren't you good?
ORLANDO. I hope so.
ROSALIND. Why then, can one desire too much of a good thing? Come, sister, you shall be the priest, and marry us. Give me your hand, Orlando. What do you say, sister?
ORLANDO. Please, marry us.
CELIA. I can't say the words.
ROSALIND. You must begin 'Will you, Orlando'—
CELIA. All right then. Will you, Orlando, take this Rosalind as your wife?
ORLANDO. I will.
ROSALIND. Yes, but when?
ORLANDO. Why, now; as fast as she can marry us.
ROSALIND. Then you must say 'I take you, Rosalind, for my wife.'
ORLANDO. I take you, Rosalind, for my wife.
ROSALIND. I might ask you for your license; but—I do take you, Orlando, for my husband. There's a girl who goes ahead of the priest; and, certainly, a woman's thought runs ahead of her actions.
ORLANDO. So do all thoughts; they are winged.
ROSALIND. Now tell me how long you would have her, after you have possessed her.
ORLANDO. Forever and a day.

ROSALIND. Say 'a day' without the 'forever.' No, no, Orlando; men are April when they woo, December when they wed. Maids are May when they are maids, but the sky changes when they are wives. I will be more jealous of you than a Barbary cock-pigeon over his hen, more clamorous than a parrot against rain, more new-fangled than an ape, more giddy in my desires than a monkey. I will weep for nothing, like Diana in the fountain, and I'll do that when you're disposed to be merry. I'll laugh like a hyena, and that when you're inclined to sleep.
ORLANDO. But will my Rosalind do so?
ROSALIND. By my life, she will do as I do.
ORLANDO. Oh, but she is wise.

ROSALIND. Or else she could not have the wit to do this. The wiser, the more wayward. Shut the door upon a woman's wit, and it will go out by the window; shut that, and it will go out at the keyhole; stop that, and it will fly with the smoke out the chimney.
ORLANDO. A man who had a wife with such a wit, he might say, 'Wit, where are you going?' ROSALIND. No, you might keep that retort for when you met your wife's wit going to your neighbor's bed.
ORLANDO. And what wit could wit have to excuse that?

ROSALIND. Marry, to say she came there to look for you. You'll never catch her without an answer, unless you take her without her tongue. Oh, that woman who can't turn her fault into her husband's occasion—let her never nurse her child herself, for she'll raise it like a fool!
ORLANDO. For these next two hours, Rosalind, I must leave you.
ROSALIND. Alas, dear love, I cannot do without you for two hours!
ORLANDO. I must attend the Duke at dinner; by two o'clock I'll be with you again.

ROSALIND. Yes, go your ways, go your ways. I knew what you would turn out to be; my friends told me as much, and I thought no less. That flattering tongue of yours won me. It's only one more woman cast away, and so—come death! Two o'clock is your hour?
ORLANDO. Yes, sweet Rosalind.

ROSALIND. By my faith, and in good earnest, and so God mend me, and by all pretty oaths that are not dangerous, if you break one jot of your promise, or come one minute behind your hour, I will think you the most pathetical break-promise, and the most hollow lover, and the most unworthy of her you call Rosalind, who may be picked out of the gross band of the unfaithful. So beware my censure, and keep your promise.
ORLANDO. With no less religion than if you were indeed my Rosalind; so, adieu.
ROSALIND. Well, Time is the old justice who examines all such offenders, and let Time try. Adieu.             Exit ORLANDO
CELIA. You have simply misused our sex in your love-prate. We must have your doublet and hose pulled over your head, and show the world what the bird has done to her own nest.

ROSALIND. Oh cousin, cousin, cousin, my pretty little cousin, if only you knew how many fathoms deep I am in love! But it can't be sounded; my affection has an unknown bottom, like the Bay of Portugal.
CELIA. Or rather, bottomless—so that as fast as you pour affection in, it runs out.

ROSALIND. No; that same wicked bastard of Venus, who was begotten of thought, conceived of spleen, and born of madness; that blind rascally boy, who abuses everyone's eyes because his own are out—let him be judge how deep I am in love. I'll tell you, Aliena, I cannot be out of the sight of Orlando. I'll go find a shadow, and sigh till he comes.
CELIA. And I'll sleep.                                  Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2
paragraphs: The forest
Enter JAQUES and LORDS, in the habit of foresters
JAQUES. Which one is he that killed the deer?
LORD. Sir, it was I.
JAQUES. Let's present him to the Duke, like a Roman conqueror; and it would be fitting to set the deer's horns upon his head as a branch of victory. Have you no song, forester, for this purpose?
LORD. Yes, sir.
JAQUES. Sing it; no matter whether it's in tune, so long as it makes noise enough.
SONG.
What shall he have that killed the deer? His leather skin and horns to wear.
[The rest shall hear this refrain:]
Then sing him home.

Take no scorn at wearing the horn; It was a crest before you were born. Your father's father wore it; And your father bore it. The horn, the horn, the lusty horn, Is not a thing to laugh to scorn.                   Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3
paragraphs: The forest
Enter ROSALIND and CELIA
ROSALIND. What do you say now? Isn't it past two o'clock? And no sign of Orlando!
CELIA. I warrant you, with pure love and troubled brain, he has taken his bow and arrows, and gone off—to sleep. Look, who comes here.
Enter SILVIUS

SILVIUS. My errand is to you, fair youth; My gentle Phebe bade me give you this. I do not know the contents; but, as I guess By the stern brow and waspish manner She had as she was writing it, It carries an angry tone. Pardon me, I am only a guiltless messenger.

ROSALIND. Patience herself would startle at this letter, And play the swaggerer. Bear this, bear all. She says I am not fair, that I lack manners; She calls me proud, and says she could not love me, Were a man as rare as a Phoenix. By my will! Her love is not the hare I am hunting; Why does she write to me like this? Well, shepherd, well, This is a letter of your own contrivance.
SILVIUS. No, I protest, I do not know the contents; Phebe did write it.

ROSALIND. Come, come, you are a fool, And turned to the extremity of love. I saw her hand; she has a leathern hand, A freestone-colored hand; I really did think Her old gloves were on, but it was her hands; She has a housewife's hand—but that's no matter. I tell you, she never invented this letter: This is a man's invention, and a man's handwriting.
SILVIUS. Sure, it is hers.

ROSALIND. Why, it's a boisterous and a cruel style; A style for challengers. Why, she defies me, Like Turk to Christian. Women's gentle brain Could not produce such giant-rude invention, Such Ethiope words, blacker in their meaning Than in their appearance. Will you hear the letter?
SILVIUS. If you please, for I have not heard it yet; Though I have heard too much of Phebe's cruelty.
ROSALIND. She Phebes me: mark how the tyrant writes.
[Reads]
'Are you a god turned shepherd, That a maiden's heart has burned?'
Can a woman rail like this?
SILVIUS. You call this railing?
ROSALIND. 'Why, with your godhead laid aside, Do you war with a woman's heart?'
Did you ever hear such railing?
'While the eye of man did woo me, That could do no harm to me.'
Meaning me, a beast.

'If the scorn of your bright eyes Have power to raise such love in mine, Alas, in me what strange effect Would they work in mild aspect! While you scolded me, I did love; How then might your prayers move me! He that brings this love to you Little knows this love in me; And by him seal up your answer, Whether your youth and kind Will take the faithful offer Of me and all that I can make; Or else by him my love deny, And then I'll study how to die.'
SILVIUS. You call this chiding?
CELIA. Alas, poor shepherd!

ROSALIND. Do you pity him? No, he deserves no pity. Will you love such a woman? What, to make you an instrument and play false notes upon you! Not to be endured! Well, go your way back to her, since I see love has made you a tame snake, and tell her this—that if she loves me, I command her to love you; if she will not, I will never have her, unless you plead for her. If you're a true lover, go—and not a word; for here comes more company. Exit SILVIUS
Enter OLIVER
OLIVER. Good morning, fair ones; please, if you know, Where in the outskirts of this forest stands A sheep-cote fenced about with olive trees?

CELIA. West of this place, down in the neighboring valley. The row of willows by the murmuring stream, Left on your right hand, brings you to the place. But at this hour the house is empty; There's no one inside.

OLIVER. If an eye may profit by a tongue, Then I should know you by description— Such garments, and such years: 'The boy is fair, Of female features, and conducts himself Like a grown sister; the woman is short, And browner than her brother.' Are you not The owners of the house I was asking after?
CELIA. It's no boast, when asked, to say we are.
OLIVER. Orlando commends himself to you both; And to that youth he calls his Rosalind He sends this bloody handkerchief. Are you he?
ROSALIND. I am. What must we understand by this?
OLIVER. Something of my shame, if you will hear from me What man I am, and how, and why, and where, This handkerchief was stained.
CELIA. Please, tell it.

OLIVER. When last young Orlando parted from you, He left a promise to return Within an hour; and, walking through the forest, Chewing on the food of sweet and bitter fancy, Lo, what happened! He cast his eye aside, And mark what object appeared. Under an oak, whose boughs were mossed with age, And high top bald with dry antiquity, A wretched ragged man, overgrown with hair, Lay sleeping on his back. About his neck A green and gilded snake had wreathed itself, Who with her head, nimble in threats, approached The opening of his mouth; but suddenly, Seeing Orlando, it unwound itself, And with zigzag glides slipped away Into a bush; under whose shade A lioness, with udders all drawn dry, Lay crouching, head on the ground, with catlike watch, Waiting for the sleeping man to stir; for it's The royal disposition of that beast To prey on nothing that seems already dead. Seeing this, Orlando did approach the man, And found it was his brother, his elder brother.
CELIA. Oh, I have heard him speak of that very brother; And he described him as the most unnatural Who lived among men.
OLIVER. And well he might do so, For well I know he was unnatural.
ROSALIND. But, of Orlando: did he leave him there, Food for the sucked-dry and hungry lioness?

OLIVER. Twice he turned his back, and meant to do so; But kindness, nobler always than revenge, And nature, stronger than his just provocation, Made him give battle to the lioness, Who quickly fell before him; in which struggle From miserable slumber I awoke.
CELIA. Are you his brother?
ROSALIND. Was it you he rescued?
CELIA. Was it you who so often contrived to kill him?
OLIVER. It was I; but it is not I now. I am not ashamed To tell you what I was, since my conversion Tastes so sweetly, being the thing I am now.
ROSALIND. But what about the bloody handkerchief?

OLIVER. In a moment. When from the first to last, between us two, Tears had most kindly bathed our accounts— Such as how I came to that desert place— In brief, he led me to the gentle Duke, Who gave me fresh clothes and entertainment, Committing me to my brother's love. He led me instantly to his cave, There stripped himself, and here upon his arm The lioness had torn away some flesh, Which all this while had bled; and now he fainted, And cried, in fainting, upon Rosalind. Briefly, I revived him, bound up his wound, And, after some short time, being strong at heart, He sent me here, stranger as I am, To tell this story, so that you might excuse His broken promise, and to give this handkerchief, Dyed in his blood, to the shepherd youth Whom he in sport calls his Rosalind.
[ROSALIND swoons]
CELIA. Why, what now, Ganymede! Sweet Ganymede!
OLIVER. Many will swoon when they look on blood.
CELIA. There's more to it. Cousin Ganymede!
OLIVER. Look, he's recovering.
ROSALIND. I wish I were at home.
CELIA. We'll lead you there. Please, will you take him by the arm?
OLIVER. Be of good cheer, youth. You, a man! You lack a man's heart.
ROSALIND. I do, I confess it. Ah, sir, anybody would think this was well counterfeited. Please tell your brother how well I counterfeited. Heigh-ho!
OLIVER. This was not counterfeit; there's too great a witness in your complexion that it was a passion in earnest.
ROSALIND. Counterfeit, I assure you.
OLIVER. Well then, take heart and counterfeit to be a man.
ROSALIND. So I do; but, in faith, I should have been a woman by right.
CELIA. Come, you look paler and paler; please, head for home. Good sir, come with us.
OLIVER. That I will, for I must carry back word How you excuse my brother, Rosalind.
ROSALIND. I shall devise something; but please, commend my counterfeiting to him. Will you come?                   Exeunt

ACT V. SCENE I. The forest
Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY
TOUCHSTONE. We shall find a time, Audrey; patience, gentle Audrey.
AUDREY. Faith, the priest was good enough, for all that the old gentleman said.
TOUCHSTONE. A most wicked Sir Oliver, Audrey, a most vile Martext. But, Audrey, there's a youth here in the forest who lays claim to you.
AUDREY. Yes, I know who it is; he has no claim on me in the world; here comes the man you mean.
Enter WILLIAM
TOUCHSTONE. It's meat and drink to me to see a clown. By my faith, we who have good wits have much to answer for: we shall be flouting; we can't hold back.
WILLIAM. Good evening, Audrey.
AUDREY. God give you good evening, William.
WILLIAM. And good evening to you, sir.
TOUCHSTONE. Good evening, gentle friend. Cover your head, cover your head; no, please, put your hat back on. How old are you, friend?
WILLIAM. Twenty-five, sir.
TOUCHSTONE. A ripe age. Is your name William?
WILLIAM. William, sir.
TOUCHSTONE. A fair name. Were you born in this forest?
WILLIAM. Yes, sir, I thank God.
TOUCHSTONE. 'Thank God.' A good answer. Are you rich?
WILLIAM. Faith, sir, so-so.
TOUCHSTONE. 'So-so' is good, very good, very excellently good; and yet it is not; it is only so-so. Are you wise?
WILLIAM. Yes, sir, I have a pretty wit.

TOUCHSTONE. Why, you say well. I now remember a saying: 'The fool thinks he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool.' The heathen philosopher, when he had a desire to eat a grape, would open his lips when he put it into his mouth; meaning thereby that grapes were made to be eaten and lips to be opened. Do you love this maid?
WILLIAM. I do, sir.
TOUCHSTONE. Give me your hand. Are you learned?
WILLIAM. No, sir.

TOUCHSTONE. Then learn this from me: to have is to have; for it is a figure in rhetoric that drink, being poured out of a cup into a glass, by filling the one empties the other; for all your writers agree that ipse is he; now, you are not ipse, for I am he.
WILLIAM. Which he, sir?

TOUCHSTONE. He, sir, who must marry this woman. Therefore, you clown, abandon—which in the vulgar tongue means leave—the society—which in boorish speech means company—of this female—which in common speech means woman—which all together comes to: abandon the society of this female; or, clown, you perish; or, in plainer words, you die; or, to wit, I kill you, do away with you, translate your life into death, your liberty into bondage. I will deal with you in poison, or in cudgeling, or in steel; I will scheme with you in faction; I will overrun you with policy; I will kill you a hundred and fifty ways; therefore tremble and depart.
AUDREY. Do, good William.
WILLIAM. God rest you merry, sir.                         Exit
Enter CORIN
CORIN. Our master and mistress are looking for you; come away, away.
TOUCHSTONE. Trip, Audrey, trip, Audrey. I'm coming, I'm coming. Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2
paragraphs: The forest
Enter ORLANDO and OLIVER

ORLANDO. Is it possible that on so little acquaintance you should like her? That just by seeing her you should love her? And, loving, woo her? And, wooing, she should accept? And do you persevere in wanting to enjoy her?

OLIVER. Don't call the giddiness of it into question, nor her poverty, nor our small acquaintance, nor my sudden wooing, nor her sudden consenting; but say with me, I love Aliena; say with her that she loves me; consent with both of us that we may enjoy each other. It shall be to your good; for my father's house and all the income that was old Sir Rowland's I'll settle on you, and here live and die a shepherd.
ORLANDO. You have my consent. Let your wedding be tomorrow. I'll invite the Duke and all his contented followers. Go and prepare Aliena; for, look you, here comes my Rosalind.
Enter ROSALIND
ROSALIND. God save you, brother.
OLIVER. And you, fair sister.                             Exit
ROSALIND. Oh, my dear Orlando, how it grieves me to see you wear your heart in a scarf!
ORLANDO. It is my arm.
ROSALIND. I thought your heart had been wounded by the claws of a lion.
ORLANDO. Wounded it is, but with the eyes of a lady.
ROSALIND. Did your brother tell you how I counterfeited a swoon when he showed me your handkerchief?
ORLANDO. Yes, and greater wonders than that.

ROSALIND. Oh, I know what you're getting at. No, it's true. There was never anything so sudden but the fight of two rams and Caesar's boastful brag of 'I came, saw, and overcame.' For your brother and my sister no sooner met than they looked; no sooner looked than they loved; no sooner loved than they sighed; no sooner sighed than they asked one another the reason; no sooner knew the reason than they sought the remedy—and by these degrees they have made a pair of stairs to marriage, which they will climb without delay, or else be without restraint before marriage. They are in the very fury of
love, and they will be together. Clubs cannot part them.

ORLANDO. They shall be married tomorrow; and I will invite the Duke to the wedding. But, oh, how bitter a thing it is to look into happiness through another man's eyes! By how much the more shall I tomorrow be at the height of heart-heaviness, by how much I shall think my brother happy in having what he wishes for.
ROSALIND. Why then, tomorrow I cannot serve your turn for Rosalind?
ORLANDO. I can live no longer by thinking.

ROSALIND. I'll weary you, then, no longer with idle talk. Know this from me then—for now I speak to some purpose—that I know you are a gentleman of good understanding. I'm not saying this so you'll have a good opinion of my knowledge, insofar as I say I know you are; nor do I labor for a greater esteem than may in some little measure draw a belief from you, to do yourself good, and not to grace me. Believe then, if you please, that I can do strange things. I have, since I was three years old, conversed with a magician, most profound in his art and yet not damnable. If you love Rosalind as near the heart as your gestures cry it out, when your brother marries Aliena, you shall marry her. I know into what straits of fortune she's been driven; and it's not impossible for me—if it doesn't seem inconvenient to you—to set her before your eyes tomorrow, human as she is, and without any danger.
ORLANDO. Are you speaking with sober meaning?

ROSALIND. By my life, I am; which I value dearly, even though I say I'm a magician. So put on your best clothes, invite your friends; for if you want to be married tomorrow, you shall; and to Rosalind, if you will.
Enter SILVIUS and PHEBE
Look, here comes a lover of mine, and a lover of hers.
PHEBE. Youth, you have done me much ungentleness By showing the letter that I wrote to you.
ROSALIND. I don't care if I have. It is my study To seem despiteful and ungentle to you. You are followed there by a faithful shepherd; Look upon him, love him; he worships you.
PHEBE. Good shepherd, tell this youth what it is to love.
SILVIUS. It is to be all made of sighs and tears; And so am I for Phebe.
PHEBE. And I for Ganymede.
ORLANDO. And I for Rosalind.
ROSALIND. And I for no woman.
SILVIUS. It is to be all made of faith and service; And so am I for Phebe.
PHEBE. And I for Ganymede.
ORLANDO. And I for Rosalind.
ROSALIND. And I for no woman.

SILVIUS. It is to be all made of fantasy, All made of passion, and all made of wishes; All adoration, duty, and observance, All humbleness, all patience, and impatience, All purity, all trial, all obedience; And so am I for Phebe.
PHEBE. And so am I for Ganymede.
ORLANDO. And so am I for Rosalind.
ROSALIND. And so am I for no woman.
PHEBE. If this is so, why blame me for loving you?
SILVIUS. If this is so, why blame me for loving you?
ORLANDO. If this is so, why blame me for loving you?
ROSALIND. Why are you saying it too: 'Why blame me for loving you?'
ORLANDO. To her who is not here, nor does not hear.
ROSALIND. Please, no more of this; it's like the howling of Irish wolves against the moon. [To SILVIUS] I will help you if I can.
[To PHEBE] I would love you if I could.—Tomorrow meet me

all together. [To PHEBE] I will marry you if ever I marry a woman, and I'll be married tomorrow. [To ORLANDO] I will satisfy you if ever I satisfied a man, and you shall be married tomorrow. [To SILVIUS] I will content you if what pleases you contents you, and you shall be married tomorrow. [To ORLANDO] As you love Rosalind, meet. [To SILVIUS] As you love Phebe, meet;—and as I love no woman, I'll meet. So, fare you well; I've left you with your orders.
SILVIUS. I'll not fail, if I live.
PHEBE. Nor I.
ORLANDO. Nor I.                                         Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3
paragraphs: The forest
Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY
TOUCHSTONE. Tomorrow is the joyful day, Audrey; tomorrow we shall be married.
AUDREY. I do desire it with all my heart; and I hope it is no dishonest desire to wish to be a woman of the world. Here come two of the banished Duke's pages.
Enter two PAGES
FIRST PAGE. Well met, honest gentleman.
TOUCHSTONE. By my faith, well met. Come, sit, sit, and a song.
SECOND PAGE. We're at your service; sit in the middle.
FIRST PAGE. Shall we plunge right into it, without hawking, or spitting, or saying we're hoarse, which are the only prologues to a bad voice?
SECOND PAGE. In faith, in faith; and both in tune, like two gypsies on one horse.

SONG. It was a lover and his lass, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, That over the green cornfield did pass In the spring time, the only pretty ring time, When birds do sing, hey ding a ding, ding. Sweet lovers love the spring.
Between the acres of the rye, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, These pretty country folks would lie, In the spring time, &c.
This carol they began that hour, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, How that a life was but a flower, In the spring time, &c.
And therefore take the present time, With a hey, and a ho, and a hey nonino, For love is crowned with the prime, In the spring time, &c.
TOUCHSTONE. Truly, young gentlemen, though there was no great matter in the ditty, yet the tune was very out of key.
FIRST PAGE. You're mistaken, sir; we kept time, we did not lose our time.
TOUCHSTONE. By my faith, yes; I count it only time lost to hear such a foolish song. God be with you; and God mend your voices. Come, Audrey.                                               Exeunt

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4
paragraphs: The forest
Enter DUKE SENIOR, AMIENS, JAQUES, ORLANDO, OLIVER, and CELIA
DUKE SENIOR. Do you believe, Orlando, that the boy Can do all this that he has promised?
ORLANDO. I sometimes believe and sometimes do not: Like those who fear what they hope, and know they fear.
Enter ROSALIND, SILVIUS, and PHEBE
ROSALIND. Patience once more, while our compact is laid out: You say, if I bring in your Rosalind, You will bestow her on Orlando here?
DUKE SENIOR. That I would, had I kingdoms to give with her.
ROSALIND. And you say you will have her when I bring her?
ORLANDO. That I would, were I king of all kingdoms.
ROSALIND. You say you'll marry me, if I am willing?
PHEBE. That I will, even if I die the hour after.
ROSALIND. But if you do refuse to marry me, You'll give yourself to this most faithful shepherd?
PHEBE. That is the bargain.
ROSALIND. You say that you'll have Phebe, if she will?
SILVIUS. Even if to have her and death were both one thing.

ROSALIND. I have promised to make all this matter even. Keep your word, O Duke, to give your daughter; You yours, Orlando, to receive his daughter; Keep your word, Phebe, that you'll marry me, Or else, refusing me, will wed this shepherd; Keep your word, Silvius, that you'll marry her If she refuses me; and from here I go, To make these doubts all even. Exeunt ROSALIND and CELIA
DUKE SENIOR. I do recognize in this shepherd boy Some lively touches of my daughter's features.

ORLANDO. My lord, the first time that I ever saw him I thought he was a brother to your daughter. But, my good lord, this boy is forest-born, And has been tutored in the rudiments Of many desperate studies by his uncle, Whom he reports to be a great magician, Hidden in the circle of this forest.
Enter TOUCHSTONE and AUDREY
JAQUES. There is, surely, another flood coming, and these couples are coming to the ark. Here comes a pair of very strange beasts which in all tongues are called fools.
TOUCHSTONE. Salutation and greeting to you all!
JAQUES. My good lord, bid him welcome. This is the motley-minded gentleman that I have so often met in the forest. He has been a courtier, he swears.

TOUCHSTONE. If anyone doubts that, let him put me to my purgation. I have trod a measure; I have flattered a lady; I have been politic with my friend, smooth with my enemy; I have ruined three tailors; I have had four quarrels, and was likely to have fought one.
JAQUES. And how was that one settled?
TOUCHSTONE. Faith, we met, and found the quarrel was upon the seventh cause.
JAQUES. How, seventh cause? My good lord, like this fellow.
DUKE SENIOR. I like him very well.

TOUCHSTONE. God reward you, sir; I wish the same for you. I press in here, sir, among the rest of the country couplers, to swear and to forswear, according as marriage binds and blood breaks. A poor virgin, sir, an ill-favored thing, sir, but my own; a poor humor of mine, sir, to take what other men would refuse. Rich honesty dwells, like a miser, sir, in a poor house; just as your pearl in your foul oyster.
DUKE SENIOR. By my faith, he is very swift and sententious.
TOUCHSTONE. After the fashion of the fool's quick bolt, sir, and such sweet diseases.
JAQUES. But, about the seventh cause: how did you find the quarrel was on the seventh cause?

TOUCHSTONE. Upon a lie seven times removed—carry yourself more becomingly, Audrey—as thus, sir. I disliked the cut of a certain courtier's beard. He sent me word that, if I said his beard was not cut well, he was of the mind that it was. This is called the Retort Courteous. If I sent him word again that it was not well cut, he would send word that he cut it to please himself. This is called the Quip Modest. If again that it was not well cut, he disparaged my judgment. This is called the Reply Churlish. If again it was not well cut, he would answer I did not speak the truth. This is called the Reproof Valiant. If again it was not well cut, he would say I lie. This is called the Countercheck Quarrelsome. And so on to the Lie Circumstantial and the Lie Direct.
JAQUES. And how often did you say his beard was not well cut?
TOUCHSTONE. I dared go no further than the Lie Circumstantial, nor did he dare give me the Lie Direct; and so we measured swords and parted.
JAQUES. Can you name in order now the degrees of the lie?

TOUCHSTONE. Oh, sir, we quarrel by the book, just as you have books for good manners. I will name you the degrees. The first, the Retort Courteous; the second, the Quip Modest; the third, the Reply Churlish; the fourth, the Reproof Valiant; the fifth, the Countercheck Quarrelsome; the sixth, the Lie with Circumstance; the seventh, the Lie Direct. All these you may avoid except the Lie Direct; and you may avoid that too with an If. I knew when seven justices could not settle a quarrel; but when the parties met themselves, one of them thought only of an If, as: 'If you
said so, then I said so.' And they shook hands, and swore brotherhood. Your If is the only peacemaker; much virtue in If.
JAQUES. Is not this a rare fellow, my lord? He's as good at anything, and yet a fool.
DUKE SENIOR. He uses his folly like a stalking-horse, and under the cover of it he shoots his wit.
Enter HYMEN, ROSALIND, and CELIA. Still MUSIC

HYMEN.    Then there is mirth in heaven, When earthly things, made even, Are reconciled together. Good Duke, receive your daughter; Hymen from heaven has brought her, Yes, brought her hither, That you might join her hand with his Whose heart is within his bosom.
ROSALIND. [To DUKE] To you I give myself, for I am yours.
[To ORLANDO] To you I give myself, for I am yours.
DUKE SENIOR. If there be truth in sight, you are my daughter.
ORLANDO. If there be truth in sight, you are my Rosalind.
PHEBE. If sight and shape be true, Why then, my love adieu!
ROSALIND. I'll have no father, if you are not he; I'll have no husband, if you are not he; Nor ever wed any woman, if you are not she.

HYMEN.    Peace, ho! I bar confusion; It is I must make the conclusion Of these most strange events. Here are eight that must take hands To join in Hymen's bands, If truth holds true contents. You and you no cross shall part; You and you are heart to heart; You to his love must accord, Or have a woman as your lord; You and you are sure together, As the winter to foul weather. While a wedlock-hymn we sing, Feed yourselves with questioning, That reason wonder may diminish— How we thus met, and these things finish.
SONG Wedding is great Juno's crown; O blessed bond of board and bed! It is Hymen who peoples every town; High wedlock then be honored. Honor, high honor, and renown, To Hymen, god of every town!
DUKE SENIOR. O my dear niece, welcome you are to me! Even as daughter, welcome in no less degree.
PHEBE. I will not eat my word, now you are mine; Your faith binds my fancy to you.
Enter JAQUES de BOYS

JAQUES de BOYS. Give me audience for a word or two. I am the second son of old Sir Rowland, Who brings these tidings to this fair assembly. Duke Frederick, hearing how every day Men of great worth resorted to this forest, Mustered a mighty force, which were on foot, Under his own command, purposely to capture His brother here, and put him to the sword. And to the edge of this wild wood he came, Where, meeting with an old religious man, After some conversation with him, was converted Both from his enterprise and from the world; His crown bequeathing to his banished brother, And all their lands restored again to those That were exiled with him. This to be true I do pledge my life.

DUKE SENIOR. Welcome, young man. You offer a fair gift to your brothers' wedding: To one, his lands withheld; and to the other, A land itself at large, a potent dukedom. First, in this forest let us complete those ends That here were well begun and well begotten; And after, every one of this happy number That has endured rough days and nights with us Shall share the good of our returned fortune, According to the measure of their stations. For now, forget this new-fallen dignity, And fall into our rustic revelry. Play, music; and you brides and bridegrooms all, With measure heaped in joy, to the measures fall.
JAQUES. Sir, by your leave. If I heard you rightly, The Duke has put on a religious life, And cast off into neglect the pompous court.
JAQUES DE BOYS. He has.
JAQUES. Then to him I will go. From these converts There is much matter to be heard and learned.
[To DUKE] You to your former honor I bequeath;
Your patience and your virtue well deserve it.
[To ORLANDO] You to a love that your true faith merits;
[To OLIVER] You to your land, and love, and great allies;
[To SILVIUS] You to a long and well-deserved bed;
[To TOUCHSTONE] And you to wrangling; for your loving voyage
Is provisioned for only two months.—So to your pleasures; I am for other things than dancing measures.
DUKE SENIOR. Stay, Jaques, stay.
JAQUES. No pastime for me to see. What you would have, I'll wait to hear at your abandoned cave.               Exit
DUKE SENIOR. Proceed, proceed. We will begin these rites, As we trust they will end, in true delights.    [A dance] Exeunt
EPILOGUE
EPILOGUE.

ROSALIND. It is not the fashion to see the lady give the epilogue; but it is no more unhandsome than to see the lord give the prologue. If it is true that good wine needs no bush, it is true that a good play needs no epilogue. Yet for good wine they do use good bushes; and good plays prove the better by the help of good epilogues. What a fix am I in then, being neither a good epilogue, nor able to insinuate with you on behalf of a good play! I am not dressed like a beggar; therefore to beg will not become me. My way is to conjure you; and I'll begin with the women. I charge you, O women, by the love you bear to men, to like as much of this play as pleases you; and I charge you, O men, by the love you bear to women—as I perceive by your simpering that none of you hates them—that between you and the women the play may please. If I were a woman, I would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased me, complexions that I liked, and breaths that I did not defy; and, I am sure, as many as have good beards, or good faces, or sweet breaths, will, for my kind offer, when I make my curtsy, bid me farewell.
